title: accesskey values must be unique
description: Checks that no two elements on the page share the same accesskey attribute value.
applicability: Applies whenever two or more elements carry a non-empty accesskey attribute: only then can two of them collide.
expectation: Every accesskey value on the page is unique. Duplicate accesskeys make keyboard-shortcut activation ambiguous: only one of the elements sharing the key can actually be reached by it, and which one is browser/platform-dependent.
reports:
- `accesskey`: the shared key, in lower case.
- `duplicateCount`: how many elements on the page share it, this one included.
- `others`: the other elements with this key, the first three, as the message names them (`<button> "Save"`).

examples.explanation: Every `accesskey` value on the page is unique.
Two elements share the same `accesskey` value ("s"), which most browsers resolve unpredictably.

title: <area> must have an accessible name
description: Checks that <area> elements have a non-empty accessible name via alt, aria-label/aria-labelledby, or title.
applicability: Applies to elements that: 1) are in a that is referenced by an (as HTML matches it: "#" and the map's id or name, case-sensitive), AND 2) carry a non-empty href (an with no href is not a hyperlink at all per the HTML spec, and has nothing for this rule to name), AND 3) the referencing is actually rendered (hidden/display:none/ visibility exclude it; aria-hidden does not, since is not a DOM descendant of ), AND 4) the itself is eligible in the accessibility tree. hidden, display:none and inert on the or its do not exclude it: neither element generates a box, so a real browser's image-map hit-testing ignores all three there (verified against Chromium and Firefox); only those mechanisms on a genuine ancestor of the whole + pairing do.
expectation: Each applicable element has a non-empty accessible name, from alt, aria-label/aria-labelledby, or title. An in a used map is always a link, so alt="" is not decorative here as it is on : an empty alt fails the same as a missing one unless another mechanism names it.

examples.explanation: The `<area>` is a link inside a used map and has a non-empty `alt`.
The `<area>` is a link (has `href`) in a used map but has no `alt`.

title: <area> text alternative must be appropriate (manual review)
description: Flags <area> elements with a non-empty text alternative (alt, aria-label, aria-labelledby or title) for human review of appropriateness. Says when the name looks like a file name, a web address, a placeholder, an "image of" opening or is very long.
applicability: Applies to elements that get a non-empty text alternative from any source: aria-labelledby (resolving to text), aria-label, alt or title. The must carry a non-empty href (otherwise it is not a hyperlink at all per the HTML spec) and belong to a that an actually references ("#" and the map's id or name, case-sensitive, as HTML matches it); an in an unused map is out of scope. The referencing must actually be rendered (hidden/display:none/ visibility exclude it; aria-hidden does not, since is not a DOM descendant of ), and the itself must be eligible: hidden, display:none and inert on the or its do not exclude it, since neither generates a box and a real browser's image-map hit-testing ignores all three there (verified against Chromium and Firefox); only those mechanisms on a genuine ancestor of the whole + pairing do. role="presentation"/"none" takes an element out unless it is focusable.
expectation: Human review is required to confirm that the provided text alternative is accurate and appropriate. Each occurrence lists every source present (data.details.sources), so the reviewer checks each one: a title or aria-label that is not the name still reaches some users. The name is also checked for what the img-alt-quality rule checks in an alt (helpers.getTextAlternativeSignal): a file name, a web address, only symbols, a placeholder or generic word, an opening that says it is an image, or more than 150 characters. Such a name gets its own summary and hint; the finding stays `cantTell`.
reports:
- `reasonCode`: `TEXT_ALTERNATIVE_REVIEW`, whatever the signal.
- `name`: the text alternative the area ends up with, taken from the first source in `sources`.
- `sources`: each source of text the area has, in the order they are used for the name: `aria-labelledby`, `aria-label`, `alt`, `title`.
- `altSignal`, and `length` and `limit` for `too-long`: what made the name look like something other than a description, as for img-alt-quality. Absent when the name is ordinary.
- `alt` (an area with an alt attribute): the alt text.

examples.explanation: The area has a non-empty text alternative in a used image map, worth confirming "Room 12" is accurate for that region. An `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby` or `title` is asked about the same way, and each occurrence lists the sources it found.
No `` references this map, so the area is never hit-tested or rendered — out of scope.

title: aria-* attributes must be permitted for the element’s role
description: Checks that every recognized aria-* attribute present on an element with an explicit role is either globally supported or supported by that role.
applicability: Applies to elements carrying at least one recognized, non-global aria-* attribute, judged against the role they actually have: an explicit valid role, else the implicit role of their tag, else, for the elements HTML-AAM maps to no role at all, nothing. A custom element with no role attribute naming a role is judged against the role its ElementInternals give it (this.attachInternals().role), its default role, as a native element is judged against its tag's.
expectation: Every recognized aria-* attribute present is either: (a) globally supported on any element (the "global" ARIA states/properties, e.g. aria-label/aria-hidden/aria-describedby), or (b) explicitly listed as a required or supported state/property for the element's role. An attribute ARIA deprecated (rather than prohibited) on the role is still allowed: it is reported as CANTTELL, so the author decides, not as a not-allowed FAIL. The same goes for an element with no role: an attribute ARIA 1.2 made no longer global (`aria-disabled`, `aria-errormessage`, `aria-haspopup`, `aria-invalid`) is CANTTELL there too. An attribute the role does not support is reported at CANTTELL as well, not FAIL. It is a WAI-ARIA violation, but the element keeps the name, role and state it has without the attribute: `<button aria-valuenow="1">Save</button>` is still a button named Save. ACT 5c01ea maps this to WAI-ARIA, and to SC 1.3.1 and 4.1.2 only as secondary requirements "less strict" than the rule. Whether SC 4.1.2 fails depends on whether the element is a control whose state or value the page meant the attribute to convey and conveys no other way (a toggle button given aria-checked instead of aria-pressed); a person settles that.
reports:
- `attr`: the aria-* attribute that is not allowed, or deprecated, on the element.
- `role` (an element with a role): the role it was judged against, explicit or implicit. Absent when the element has no role at all.

examples.explanation: `aria-checked` is one of the states role="checkbox" supports.

`aria-valuenow` belongs to range widgets, not role="checkbox": a WAI-ARIA violation. The checkbox keeps its name, role and state without it, so whether WCAG 4.1.2 fails depends on what the attribute was meant to convey.

title: Explicit role must be permitted for its host element
description: Checks that an explicit role="" attribute is one of the roles the ARIA-in-HTML specification permits for the host element (e.g. role="tab" is not permitted on <nav>).
applicability: Applies to elements with an explicit, valid, non-abstract role, where the host element/attribute combination has an asserted permitted-roles constraint in the ARIA in HTML specification's table of permitted roles.
expectation: The explicit role is one of the roles the ARIA-in-HTML specification permits for that host element. Reported at CANTTELL rather than FAIL: ARIA-in-HTML's permitted-roles table is an author conformance requirement with no ACT rule and no WCAG mapping in any source. The role the author asked for is still the role assistive technology exposes, so whether the combination harms anyone depends on the widget, not on the table.
reports: - `role`: the explicit role that is not permitted on the host element.

examples.explanation: `role="navigation"` is permitted on `<nav>` by the ARIA-in-HTML spec (it's also the element's implicit role).
`role="tab"` is not one of the roles ARIA-in-HTML permits on `<nav>`.

title: aria-braillelabel/aria-brailleroledescription must have a non-braille equivalent
description: Checks that elements using aria-braillelabel also have a regular accessible name, and elements using aria-brailleroledescription also have aria-roledescription.
applicability: Elements with a non-empty `aria-braillelabel` and/or non-empty `aria-brailleroledescription` attribute.
expectation:
Per the ARIA specification, `aria-braillelabel` is a Braille-specific SUPPLEMENT to (not a replacement for) the element's regular accessible name, and `aria-brailleroledescription` is a supplement to `aria-roledescription`. An element must therefore also have:

- a non-empty accessible name from a non-braille mechanism, if it declares `aria-braillelabel`;
- a non-empty `aria-roledescription`, if it declares `aria-brailleroledescription`.

Using either braille-specific attribute as the ONLY naming mechanism leaves non-braille assistive technology (most screen readers, voice control, etc.) with no accessible name/role description at all. Reported at CANTTELL rather than FAIL: aria-brailleroledescription without aria-roledescription reaches no user at all, and a missing accessible name is the naming rules' decision for the roles that require one. The braille attribute being unpaired is worth surfacing, but it is not itself a criterion failing.
reports:
- `attr`: the braille attribute that has no equivalent: `aria-braillelabel` or `aria-brailleroledescription`.
- `requires`: what the element also needs: "an accessible name" for `aria-braillelabel`, `aria-roledescription` for `aria-brailleroledescription`.

examples.explanation: The braille label supplements a real accessible name ("Save changes"); non-braille assistive technology still gets a name.
`aria-braillelabel` is the only naming mechanism present; non-braille assistive technology gets no accessible name at all.

title: Native checkbox/radio aria-checked should match its actual state
description: Flags a native <input type="checkbox">/<input type="radio"> whose explicit aria-checked value disagrees with its actual checked/indeterminate state, for manual review.
applicability: Native `<input type="checkbox">` / `<input type="radio">` elements that carry an explicit `aria-checked` attribute.
expectation: `aria-checked` is redundant on a native checkbox/radio (the role's checked state is already exposed natively), but when an author sets it explicitly it should agree with the element's actual state, otherwise assistive technology is told something different from what a sighted user perceives.
reports:
- `ariaChecked`: the state `aria-checked` announces: `true`, `false`, or `mixed` (a checkbox only). A value that is not one of these counts as `false`.
- `actualState`: the state the control is really in: `true`, `false`, or `mixed` for an indeterminate checkbox.
- `type`: `checkbox` or `radio`.

examples.explanation: `aria-checked` matches the control's real checked state.
The checkbox is actually checked, but `aria-checked="false"` tells assistive technology the opposite.

title: aria-errormessage requires aria-invalid to be set to a non-false value
description: Checks that elements with aria-errormessage also have aria-invalid set to "true", "grammar", or "spelling"; otherwise the error message is dropped from the accessibility tree.
applicability: Elements with a non-empty `aria-errormessage` attribute.
expectation: Per the ARIA specification, `aria-errormessage` is only exposed to assistive technology when `aria-invalid` is present with a value other than `"false"` (i.e. `"true"`, `"grammar"`, or `"spelling"`). An element with `aria-errormessage` but `aria-invalid` absent or `"false"` silently drops the error message from the accessibility tree, authors almost always intend it to be exposed. Any other value (aria-invalid="yes") is read as "true", as WAI-ARIA 1.2 requires of a value not in its list, so the message is exposed and the element passes; the value itself is `aria-valid-attr-value`'s finding. Reported at CANTTELL rather than FAIL: aria-errormessage is only exposed once aria-invalid is set, so the reference is currently inert. Whether that costs the user anything depends on whether the message is conveyed some other way (visible text next to the field, aria-describedby), which static markup does not settle.
reports: - `ariaInvalid`: the element's `aria-invalid` value, lowercased; an empty string when the attribute is absent.

examples.html: Enter a valid email address.
examples.explanation: `aria-invalid="true"` means `aria-errormessage` is actually exposed to assistive technology.

examples.html: Enter a valid email address.
examples.explanation: Without `aria-invalid` set to a non-`"false"` value, `aria-errormessage` is never exposed — the reference is currently inert.

title: role attribute should not use a deprecated or author-discouraged ARIA role
description: Checks that an explicit role="" attribute does not use a role deprecated by the WAI-ARIA specification, or one reserved for user-agent-internal use (e.g. role="generic").
applicability: Applies to any element whose role attribute's first (used) token is a valid, non-abstract ARIA role that authors should not explicitly declare, either because WAI-ARIA has deprecated it (e.g. "directory", superseded by role="list") or because it is reserved for user-agent- internal use (role="generic", which ARIA 1.2 §5.4 says authors SHOULD NOT use in content).
expectation:
The role in use is neither deprecated nor reserved. Graded by the strength of the rule ARIA states:

- CANTTELL at SHOULD NOT, which leaves the usage conforming, so the author decides whether it matters: a deprecated role ("directory") or one reserved for user agents ("generic").
- FAIL at MUST NOT. No ARIA 1.2 or 1.3 role carries an author MUST NOT outside the abstract roles, so this outcome is reserved for a later revision promoting a role to that strength.

Distinct, atomic decision from aria-roles-valid (existence/ abstractness): a role can be valid and non-abstract while still being discouraged in explicit author use.
reports:
- `role`: the deprecated or reserved role in use.
- `guidance`: advice on what to use instead, as English text.

examples.explanation: `role="list"` is current, non-deprecated ARIA.
`role="directory"` is deprecated in WAI-ARIA in favor of `role="list"`; still valid markup, but discouraged.

title: aria-expanded should match whether the controlled content is shown
description: Flags an element whose aria-expanded value disagrees with whether the elements its aria-controls names are shown, for manual review.
expectation:
`aria-expanded` tells assistive technology whether the content the element controls is shown. When it says the opposite of what the page shows, a screen reader user is told a panel is closed while it is open, or the other way round.

- `aria-expanded="false"`, and every element `aria-controls` names is shown: cantTell (`EXPANDED_FALSE_CONTROLLED_SHOWN`).
- `aria-expanded="true"`, and every element `aria-controls` names is hidden: cantTell (`EXPANDED_TRUE_CONTROLLED_HIDDEN`).
- Otherwise: pass.

An element counts as hidden when it is out of the accessibility tree: `display: none`, `visibility: hidden`, `hidden`, a closed `<details>`, `content-visibility: hidden`, `inert` or `aria-hidden="true"` on it or an ancestor, and, in a browser, a box of its own collapsed to no height or width with its overflow clipped (an accordion panel animated with `height: 0`). A panel collapsed some other way (a transform, an ancestor's height) counts as shown, and the content a control expands may stay in view while collapsed (a paragraph cut to two lines by `line-clamp`), which is why a finding is a question.
reports:
- `ariaExpanded`: `true` or `false`, as the attribute says.
- `controlledCount`: how many elements `aria-controls` names that were compared.
- `controlled`: each of them, `{ element }` (`#menu`), and for hidden content what hides it, `hiddenBy` (`display: none`, `hidden`, `aria-hidden="true"`...) with `hiddenByElement` when an ancestor carries it.

examples.html: Orders ship within two working days.
examples.explanation: The panel is hidden, as `aria-expanded="false"` says.

examples.html: Orders ship within two working days.
examples.explanation: `aria-expanded="false"` tells a screen reader the panel is closed, but it is shown. A person checks whether the panel is open, or whether the control only expands content that stays in view.

title: The document <body> must not be aria-hidden
description: Checks that <body> does not have aria-hidden="true", which would remove the entire page from the accessibility tree.
applicability: Always applicable to any HTML document with a <body> element, independent of contextSelector/root scoping, this is a whole- document concern, matching page-title-present's pattern of evaluating document.body directly rather than the scoped root.
expectation: <body> does not have aria-hidden="true". Hiding the document body removes the entire page's content and structure from the accessibility tree at once, both 1.3.1 (Info and Relationships: the page's structure becomes entirely non-determinable) and 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value: nothing in the document exposes a role/name/value any longer) apply.

examples.explanation: The document `<body>` is not `aria-hidden`.
Hiding `<body>` removes the entire page from the accessibility tree at once.

title: ARIA hidden elements must not be focusable
description: Checks that aria-hidden="true" elements are not focusable and do not contain focusable descendants.
applicability: Applies to elements that have aria-hidden="true", the value read in any case and with surrounding whitespace ignored (aria-hidden="TRUE" hides content in browsers too).
expectation: No element with aria-hidden="true" may itself be focusable, and no focusable element may exist within an aria-hidden="true" subtree.
reports:
- `metrics.focusableTotal`: how many focusable elements the hidden element holds, counting itself if it is focusable.
- `metrics.focusableDescendants`: how many of those are inside it.
- `metrics.rootIsFocusable`: whether the hidden element itself can take focus.
- `offenders`: up to 5 of the focusable elements. Each item gives its `tag`, its `tabindex`, its `href` (a link), its `type` (an input) and its `visibilityHints`. `metrics.offendersCaptured` is how many are listed.
- `metrics.visibilityHints`: ways the focusable elements are made invisible while still taking focus: `opacityZero`, `offscreen`, `clipped`, `zeroSizeOverflowHidden`. Such an element is a focus stop a sighted keyboard user cannot see.
- `metrics.modalOpen`: whether a modal dialog was open elsewhere on the page, which turns the finding into one to review.
- `runtimeProbe`: `null` unless focusing the one focusable element moved focus straight out of the hidden element. Then it holds `redirected: true`, the tag and id of the element focus moved to (`redirectedToTag`, `redirectedToId`) and `focusTrace`, the elements focus passed through. A hidden focus sentinel that hands focus on like this is reported for review.

examples.explanation: Nothing inside the hidden subtree is focusable, so hiding it from assistive tech leaves no dead focus stop.
The link stays in the tab order even though `aria-hidden` removes it from the accessibility tree.

title: aria-owns must give each element one owner, and never an ancestor of the owner
description: Checks that no element is named by more than one aria-owns, and that no aria-owns names the element itself or one of its ancestors.
applicability: Elements the page shows with an `aria-owns` naming at least one element in the same tree.
expectation:
WAI-ARIA: an element has only one owner, so its id is in no more than one `aria-owns`, and an element cannot own one that contains it.

- An element named by two or more `aria-owns`: fail (`ARIA_OWNS_DUPLICATE`), reported on the element owned. The browser gives it to one owner, by order, so the structure the other owners state is lost.
- An `aria-owns` naming the element itself or one of its ancestors: cantTell (`ARIA_OWNS_ANCESTOR`), reported on the owner. The ownership is impossible (it would make a cycle) and is ignored, so the structure the document itself states still stands: the WAI-ARIA violation is certain, but a relationship the page shows is lost only if it differs from that structure, which a person settles.
- Otherwise: pass.
reports:
- `ownerCount`: for `ARIA_OWNS_DUPLICATE`, how many elements name the owned element in `aria-owns`.
- `ownedId`: the id named.

title: ARIA naming attributes must not be used on roles that prohibit them
description: Checks that aria-label/aria-labelledby are not present on WAI-ARIA roles whose specification explicitly prohibits ARIA naming (e.g. generic, emphasis, strong, paragraph).
applicability:
Applies to (a) elements whose explicit, valid role is one of the ARIA 1.2 roles with a documented "Prohibited ARIA States and Properties" list for naming attributes (pure text-semantics / non-naming structural roles: caption, code, deletion, emphasis, generic, insertion, mark, none, paragraph, presentation, strong, subscript, suggestion, superscript, time), plus a native with no valid explicit role, whose implicit role is caption, and (b) elements with no role at all: native HTML tags verified to carry no implicit role (such as
, ,

, , , and ), or any autonomous custom element (a hyphenated, author-defined tag per the Custom Elements spec). In both cases, only elements that also carry aria-label or aria-labelledby. A custom element whose ElementInternals give it a role (this.attachInternals().role) is judged by that role, its default role: one of the roles above puts it in (a), any other keeps it out of (b).
expectation: Prohibited attributes must not be present on (a); for (b), the naming attribute is at best unreliable (nothing accessible-name-aware to hang it off) and at worst silently ignored by assistive technology. A roleless element whose own content already gives it a name is reported as CANTTELL, since the attribute may be a deliberate override; one with no other source for a name FAILs. The same holds for (a): an element whose own text already names it loses nothing WCAG requires for certain when the prohibited label is ignored, so the WAI-ARIA violation is reported at CANTTELL (ACT kb1m8s maps it to WAI-ARIA, with SC 1.3.1 only as a secondary requirement); without such text it FAILs. A role description on generic or on an element with no role refines no control, so it is a WAI-ARIA violation reported at CANTTELL whatever the content.
reports:
- `attr`: the naming attribute found, `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.
- `role`: the role that prohibits it; `null` on an element with no role.

examples.explanation: role="generic" cannot be named, and none of the naming attributes are present.
`aria-label` is set on a role that WAI-ARIA prohibits from being named.

title: Container roles must not own a child with a disallowed role
description: Checks that every accessible-tree-owned child of a container role (list, listbox, menu, menubar, radiogroup, rowgroup, table, grid, treegrid, tablist, tree, row) has one of that role's allowed owned roles.
applicability: Applies to elements with an explicit, valid role that is one of the container roles with a documented "required owned elements" entry (the same table aria-required-children uses).
expectation: Every accessible-tree-owned descendant of the container (after pruning role="none"/"presentation" elements, and any "group"/ "rowgroup" wrapper the container's own required-owned set names, as transparent for owned-element matching per WAI-ARIA, regardless of whether "group"/"rowgroup" is itself in the container's own required-owned-roles set) has a role from that same required-owned set. Nothing else is a structurally valid direct child of a composite/container role, where "allowed" is the container's required-owned roles plus a small set of roles it may own without being required to (a separator between menu items, a caption on a grid). A roleless wrapper is descended into to reach the items a component library buries inside it, but once one is found there the rest of that wrapper's subtree is the item's own content and is not judged against the container.
reports:
- `containerRole`: the container's role.
- `containerSelector`: a selector for the container.
- `allowedOwnedRoles`: the roles the container may own. Each item is a role name.
- `childRole` (a child with a role): the child's role, which is not one of them; for a link, a button or another control focusable by itself, the role its element has (`link`, `button`). `null` on a child with no role.
- `attr` (a child with no role, or one focusable by itself): what makes it a node of its own: the global aria-* attribute it carries, `tabindex`, or `nativeFocusable` when it can take focus without one (a link, a button).

examples.explanation: Both owned children are roles menubar's spec allows.

title: Roles with a required ARIA state/property must carry it
description: Checks that elements with an explicit role carry every unambiguous, context-independent required aria-* state/property for that role (e.g. role="checkbox" must have aria-checked).
applicability: Applies to elements with an explicit, valid, non-abstract role that is also one of the small set of roles with a documented, context- independent required state/property (checkbox, combobox, heading, menuitemcheckbox, menuitemradio, meter, radio, scrollbar, separator, slider, switch) -- except when that explicit role is identical to the element's own native/implicit role (ACT 4e8ab6: e.g. <input type="checkbox" role="checkbox">, which is exempt because the native control's own state exposure already covers it; no aria-checked is required. helpers.aria.getNativeRoleForElement resolves this). A native <input type="checkbox"> or <input type="radio"> with another checkable role (switch, menuitemcheckbox, menuitemradio, or checkbox on a radio and the reverse) is in scope, but its aria-checked counts as supplied: the browser exposes the input's own checked state (HTML-AAM), so it passes without the attribute.
expectation:
Every required state/property for that role is present and non-empty. Graded by whether ARIA supplies a stand-in for the missing attribute:

- FAIL where it does not, so the state is simply not exposed (aria-checked on checkbox/radio/switch/menuitemcheckbox/menuitemradio, aria-valuenow on slider/scrollbar/meter and on a focusable separator).
- CANTTELL where ARIA defines an implicit value the role falls back to (aria-expanded on combobox, aria-level on heading), so the role still exposes a value and only the author knows whether it is the right one.
reports:
- `attr`: the required attribute that is missing or empty.
- `role`: the element's role.
- `implicitValue` (the CANTTELL case): the value ARIA falls back to, `false` for aria-expanded on a combobox, `2` for aria-level on a heading.

examples.explanation: role="checkbox" requires `aria-checked`, and it's present.
role="checkbox" requires `aria-checked`; it's missing entirely.

title: Container roles must own at least one required child role
description: Checks that container roles with a documented "required owned elements" entry (list, listbox, menu, radiogroup, table, grid, tablist, tree, row, ...) contain at least one descendant or aria-owns-referenced element with an acceptable owned role.
applicability: Applies to elements with an explicit, valid, non-abstract role that is also one of the container roles with a documented "required owned elements" entry (list, listbox, menu, menubar, radiogroup, rowgroup, table, grid, treegrid, tablist, tree, row). The container needs its explicit role, but an owned element may take its role from a custom element's ElementInternals (this.attachInternals().role), as an owned native element takes its tag's.
expectation: At least one descendant, or one aria-owns-referenced element, has one of the acceptable owned roles for that container role. A container with none that owns text, directly or through generic wrappers (a <span> or <div> with no role), FAILS: the text sits where its required children belong, as in a list whose items have no role (ACT bc4a75, Failed Example 1). One that owns nothing is asked about (CANTTELL): it conveys nothing false -- an empty role="list" is announced as a list with no items, which is what it is, and a script may fill it. Whether the content a container does own is VALID is aria-prohibited-children's decision, and that rule still fails, so a genuinely misdescribed structure (a role="button" among list items, a tablist of plain buttons) is caught with the same strength as before. The native-HTML equivalents already work this way: nothing in this ruleset fails an empty <ul>, and list-children-valid judges only the children that exist.
reports:
- `role`: the container's role.
- `requiredOwnedRoles`: the roles it needs at least one child with. Each item is a role name.

examples.explanation: The list role owns at least one `listitem`-role child.
An empty `role="list"` owns no required child role — announced as a list with no items, which is what it is, but worth a look.

title: Roles requiring a specific context role must be in that context
description: Checks that roles with a documented "required context role" entry (listitem, option, tab, treeitem, row, cell, ...) have an ancestor or aria-owns owner with an acceptable context role.
applicability: Applies to elements with an explicit, valid, non-abstract role that is also one of the roles with a documented, non-empty "required context role" entry (listitem, option, menuitem, menuitemcheckbox, menuitemradio, tab, treeitem, row, cell, gridcell, columnheader, rowheader, rowgroup). The element needs its explicit role, but its context may take its role from a custom element's ElementInternals (this.attachInternals().role), as a native context takes its tag's.
expectation: The element has an ancestor (DOM containment) or owner (via that ancestor/owner's aria-owns) whose effective role is one of the acceptable context roles for this element's role.
reports:
- `role`: the element's role.
- `requiredContextRoles`: the roles one of which it must sit inside, or be owned by. Each item is a role name.

examples.explanation: role="tab" requires an ancestor (or `aria-owns` owner) with role="tablist", and one is present.
role="tab" has no tablist ancestor or owner anywhere on the page.

title: ARIA roles that require an accessible name have one
description: Checks that the ARIA roles WAI-ARIA requires an accessible name for expose a non-empty one.
applicability: Applies to elements whose role attribute resolves to one of grid, meter, progressbar, radiogroup or tree (its first token naming a known role, matched in any case: role="foo tree" and role="TREE" count, role="link tree" does not), and that are included in the accessibility tree. Membership is decided by WAI-ARIA's own "Accessible Name Required: True" characteristic, not by whether a role merely permits a name: tablist, toolbar, menu, menubar and scrollbar are name-from-author roles the spec does not require a name for, and are out of scope. meter and progressbar are also covered by meter-name-present and progressbar-name-present, which map to SC 1.1.1; this rule is what gives those two roles their 4.1.2 coverage. A custom element whose ElementInternals give it one of those roles (this.attachInternals().role), with no role attribute naming another, is in scope too: that is its default role, and no other rule checks it. A variant with the setting roles: 'all' also checks application, marquee, table, tabpanel and treegrid, the other name-from-author roles WAI-ARIA requires a name for: a standard for WAI-ARIA asks it, and a WCAG scan does not, as an unnamed table is common and usually no WCAG failure.
expectation: The element has a non-empty aria-label, an aria-labelledby that resolves to non-empty text, or a non-empty title. Every role in the set is name-from-author-only, so descendant text is not accepted: a labelled child inside a composite widget would otherwise pass the container that has no name of its own. The name the HTML host element gives itself counts too, since the browser still computes it under the role: the first child <legend> of a <fieldset>, the first child <caption> of a <table>, and an associated <label> on a labelable element such as <progress> or <meter>. A missing name is reported at CANTTELL, not FAIL. The requirement is WAI-ARIA's ("Accessible Name Required: True"), and none of these roles is by itself a user interface component in WCAG's sense, "a single control for a distinct function": a grid, tree or radiogroup is a container of controls (its cells, items or radios, each named by its own rule), and a meter or progressbar is no control at all. So a missing name proves the WAI-ARIA violation, not a failure of SC 4.1.2. It can still be one, or a failure of another criterion, depending on the page: a visible question above a radiogroup that is not tied to it, a visible title for a grid that is not tied to it. A person settles that. A meter or progressbar with no text alternative fails SC 1.1.1 through meter-name-present and progressbar-name-present.
reports: - `role`: the role that needs a name, one of `grid`, `meter`, `progressbar`, `radiogroup` and `tree`. A stable contract, unlike the rest of `data.details`.

examples.explanation: role="grid" requires an accessible name, and `aria-label` provides one.

role="grid" requires an accessible name in WAI-ARIA; none is present. A grid is a container of controls, not a single control, so whether a WCAG criterion fails depends on whether the page shows a title for it that is not tied to it.

title: role attribute must be a valid, non-abstract ARIA role
description: Checks that an explicit role="" attribute resolves to a real, non-abstract WAI-ARIA role.
applicability: Applies to any element with a non-empty role="" attribute in the composed DOM.
expectation:
At least one role token names a concrete, non-abstract ARIA role. Graded by what the element falls back to when none does:

- FAIL on a roleless host (div, span, custom element) that takes focus, which is left exposed as generic: a control whose role is not programmatically determinable (SC 4.1.2, F59).
- CANTTELL on a roleless host that takes no focus. The WAI-ARIA violation is certain, but whether losing the role the author meant fails a criterion depends on the page: `<div role="heding">` fails SC 1.3.1 only if it is shown as a heading. ACT 674b10 maps the rule to no WCAG requirement for conformance.
- CANTTELL where the element has a native role (a <button>, <nav>, <a href>), which the accessibility tree keeps using. ACT 674b10 lists 4.1.2 as a secondary requirement only, "satisfied through the implicit role," so the bad token is worth reporting but is not itself the criterion failing.
reports:
- `role`: the first token of the role attribute. No token in it is a known role, or the known ones are all abstract.
- `nativeRole` (the CANTTELL case): the element's native role, which assistive technology keeps using.

examples.explanation: "button" is a real, concrete ARIA role.
"buton" isn't a defined ARIA role token (typo), so a control that takes focus is left with no role.
"heding" isn't a defined ARIA role token either, but the element takes no focus: whether losing the heading role fails WCAG depends on whether the page shows it as a heading.

title: role="text" elements should have no focusable descendants
description: Checks that elements with role="text" contain no focusable descendant (link, button, form control, tabindex, iframe, or contenteditable).
applicability: Elements whose role attribute has the token `text`, matched in any case, before any token naming a WAI-ARIA role, so `role="foo text"` and `role="TEXT"` count while `role="link text"` (a link) does not.
expectation: `role="text"` names no WAI-ARIA role (neither WAI-ARIA 1.2 nor the 1.3 draft defines it; aria-roles-valid reports it), but some assistive technology has read it as asking to treat an element's whole subtree as a single unit of plain text (e.g. text visually split across multiple `<span>`s by styling). That only makes sense when the subtree contains no focusable content: a focusable descendant inside a "this is just text" region is unreachable or confusing for keyboard/AT users.
reports: - `focusableElement`, `focusableSelector`: the first focusable element inside, as the message names it (`<a> "details"`) and a selector.

examples.html: Plain text with no interactive content.
examples.explanation: No focusable descendant exists inside the `role="text"` element.

examples.html: Some text with a link inside it.
examples.explanation: `role="text"` is meant to have the content read as a single flat string, but the nested link is still focusable and interactive underneath it.

title: aria-* attributes must be real, defined ARIA attributes
description: Checks that every aria-* attribute name present in the DOM is a real attribute defined by the WAI-ARIA specification.
applicability: Applies to any element in the composed DOM that carries at least one attribute whose name starts with "aria-".
expectation: Each aria-* attribute name is a real attribute defined by the WAI-ARIA specification (catches typos / made-up attribute names, which are silently ignored by assistive technology and therefore a real, deterministic defect). Reported at CANTTELL rather than FAIL: an aria-* attribute the spec does not define is inert, so nothing about the element's exposed name, role or value changes because it is there. Where the author meant a real attribute and the element ends up without a name, that absence is the naming rules' decision, not this one's. ACT 5f99a7 maps 1.3.1/4.1.2 as secondary requirements, "less strict" than the rule itself.
reports: - `attr`: the aria-* attribute name that WAI-ARIA does not define.

examples.explanation: `aria-label` is a real, defined ARIA attribute.
`aria-labeledby` is a typo (the real attribute is `aria-labelledby`) and is silently ignored by assistive technology.

title: aria-* attribute values must match their declared type
description: Checks that every recognized aria-* attribute has a value conforming to its WAI-ARIA-declared value type (boolean, tristate, token, integer, number, or ID reference).
applicability: Applies to any element carrying at least one recognized aria-* attribute (unrecognized attribute names are aria-valid-attr's concern, not evaluated here).
expectation:
Each attribute's value conforms to its WAI-ARIA-declared value type: boolean ("true"/"false"), tristate ("true"/"false"/"mixed"), a token from a fixed enumerated set, an integer (within the range WAI-ARIA sets for it), a real number, or an ID reference (list) that resolves to an existing element in the document. Boolean, tristate and token values are read in any case, as Chromium reads them (aria-checked="TRUE" is checked). Per ACT 6a7281's own applicability ("any state or property that is NOT empty"), an explicitly empty value, including a bare boolean-style attribute with no "=value" at all, e.g. `aria-checked` alone, is out of scope for every value type, not a violation: a common, deliberate pattern in templated markup (e.g. React conditionally rendering `aria-describedby={hasError ? errorId : ''}`). A value of the wrong type is a WAI-ARIA violation, which ACT 6a7281 says is "not required for conformance to WCAG 2.1 at any level". It is a FAIL only where it leaves a control's user-settable state or value, or the focused item, unstated, which SC 4.1.2 requires to be programmatically determinable: one of aria-checked, aria-pressed, aria-selected, aria-expanded or aria-valuenow on an element with a widget role, or any invalid aria-activedescendant. Anywhere else it is CANTTELL. Some attributes also constrain each other, checked once each is valid on its own:

- On an element whose role is slider, scrollbar, progressbar, meter, separator or spinbutton: `aria-valuemin` greater than `aria-valuemax` fails (`ARIA_VALUE_RANGE_INVERTED`), and so does an `aria-valuenow` outside the range (`ARIA_VALUENOW_OUT_OF_RANGE`), since the browser then gives assistive technology the nearest end of the range instead (Chromium announces 10 for 50 of 0 to 10). The range is the stated one; else a native element's own (a `<progress>`, `<meter>`, range or number input, by its `min` and `max`), as HTML-AAM maps it; else ARIA's defaults of 0 and 100, except on a spinbutton, which has none. With `aria-valuetext`, which is announced in place of the number, the value is not compared.
- `aria-posinset` greater than `aria-setsize` fails (`ARIA_POSINSET_EXCEEDS_SETSIZE`); a set size of -1 (unknown) is left alone.
- `aria-haspopup` whose popup, an element `aria-controls` names (or one inside it), has another role: cantTell (`ARIA_HASPOPUP_ROLE_MISMATCH`), as a script may show another popup. `true` means `menu`. Compared only when a named element has a role.
- `aria-activedescendant` naming an element that is neither inside the element nor inside one it names in `aria-owns` or `aria-controls`: cantTell (`ARIA_ACTIVEDESCENDANT_OUTSIDE`). A combobox is left out, as its options are in the popup it controls.
reports:
- `attr`: the attribute whose value is not valid.
- `value`: its value as written.
- `valueReason`: what is wrong with it. On an ARIA_ATTR_VALUE_INVALID finding (either tier): `expected-true-false`, `expected-true-false-undefined`, `expected-true-false-mixed`, `expected-integer`, `expected-number` or `invalid-token` when it is not of the attribute's type, `integer-out-of-range` when it is below the lowest value ARIA allows, `expected-single-idref` when an attribute taking one id holds several, `idref-not-found` when aria-activedescendant's id matches no element. On a CANTTELL: `idref-list-none-found` when none of the ids in a list matches an element, `idref-controls-not-found` for the same on aria-controls.
- For the constraints between attributes, the values compared: `role`, `valuenow`, `valuemin`, `valuemax` (the range used, defaults included); `posinset`, `setsize`; `haspopup`, `expectedRole`, `popupRole`; `activedescendant`.

examples.explanation: "true" is a valid value for the boolean-typed `aria-hidden`.
`aria-checked` is tristate; "yes" isn't a valid token, so the checkbox's checked state is not stated.
`aria-hidden` is boolean-typed; "yes" isn't a valid boolean token. It carries no control's state, so whether a WCAG criterion fails depends on the page.

title: autocomplete attribute must be a valid autofill value
description: Checks that a non-empty autocomplete attribute is "on"/"off" or a well-formed autofill detail token list.
applicability: Applies to form controls (input, select, textarea) with a non-empty autocomplete attribute. Disabled controls (the disabled attribute, including a control disabled by a disabled fieldset ancestor, or aria-disabled="true") and input types with a fixed value are exempt, as in ACT 73f2c2.
expectation: The value is "on"/"off" alone, or a well-formed autofill detail token list: an optional "section-*" token, then an optional "shipping"/"billing" token, then an optional contact-modality token (home/work/mobile/fax/pager), then exactly one recognized field-name token (name, email, street-address, cc-number, tel, ...), optionally followed by "webauthn". A malformed value means the field is not reliably identified for assistive technology that relies on autocomplete to describe the expected input purpose.
reports: - `value`: the autocomplete value as written, trimmed.

examples.explanation: "email" is a recognized autofill field-name token.
"emial" is a typo, not a recognized autofill token.

title: Inline style must not keep users from increasing text spacing
description: Checks that where inline style forces line-height, letter-spacing or word-spacing with !important, the value already reaches the spacing users must be able to apply (line-height 1.5, letter-spacing 0.12em, word-spacing 0.16em), so the user has nothing left to override.
applicability: Applies to a rendered element with visible text of its own whose style attribute declares line-height, letter-spacing or word-spacing as `!important` with a real value. A CSS-wide keyword (inherit, initial, unset, revert) specifies no spacing of its own and is out of scope.
expectation: Each such declaration already meets WCAG 1.4.12's own metric for that property, as a multiple of the font size: line-height at least 1.5, letter-spacing at least 0.12, word-spacing at least 0.16. A forced value that already satisfies the criterion leaves the user nothing to override.
reports: - `properties`: the spacing properties the finding is about. Each item is `line-height`, `letter-spacing` or `word-spacing`. On a FAIL, or on text that may never wrap, they are the ones forced below the metric; on `INLINE_SPACING_NOT_RESOLVABLE`, the ones whose value could not be worked out.

examples.explanation: The forced letter-spacing is above the WCAG 1.4.12 minimum metric.

examples.html: The toy brought back fond memories of being lost in the rain forest.
examples.explanation: `!important` forces line-height below the 1.5 minimum, and the page's own styles can't override it.
The text is short enough to fit on one line, so it may never wrap, and the criterion applies only to text that wraps.

title: Binary controls have an accessible name
description: Checks that checkbox, radio, and switch controls expose a non-empty accessible name.
applicability: Applies to elements whose role attribute resolves to checkbox, radio or switch (the first token naming a known role, matched case-insensitively, so role="foo switch" and role="SWITCH" count) that are included in the accessibility tree. A native <input type="checkbox">/<input type="radio"> is in scope only when it carries one of those roles explicitly; without a role attribute it belongs to form-control-programmatic-label-present. A custom element whose ElementInternals give it one of those roles (this.attachInternals().role), with no role attribute naming another, is in scope too: that is its default role, and no other rule checks it.
expectation: The control has a non-empty accessible name from aria-label, from an aria-labelledby that resolves to non-empty text, or from title. A native checkbox or radio additionally accepts an associated <label>, the labels API, a wrapping <label>, or label[for], with at most four labels read for determinism, and any other element accepts its own subtree text, those roles being name-from-content.

examples.explanation: `aria-label` gives the switch an accessible name.
The switch has no name from any supported mechanism.

title: Buttons have an accessible name
description: Checks that buttons expose a non-empty accessible name.
applicability: Applies to <button>, <input type="button">, <input type="submit">, <input type="reset"> and elements whose role attribute resolves to button (its first known, non-abstract token, in any case, so role="foo button" counts and role="link button" does not), where the element is included in the accessibility tree. role="presentation"/"none" takes an element out of scope unless a global ARIA attribute or focusability restores its role, per presentational roles conflict resolution. A custom element whose ElementInternals give it the button role (this.attachInternals().role), with no role attribute naming another, counts as a native element with that role does.
expectation: The element has a non-empty accessible name. A programmatic name is taken first (aria-labelledby, aria-label, an associated

Its `mechanism` is the source it stopped at, `none` when there was none, and its `flags` say why a naming attribute that is there gave no name, for example `aria-label-empty` or `aria-labelledby-empty-or-unresolvable`.

title: Page must provide a way to bypass repeated blocks
description: Checks that the page has at least one recognized mechanism to bypass blocks of repeated content: a main landmark, a working skip link, or a heading.
applicability: Applicable to any HTML document with a <body> element that is a page of its own (a document shown in a frame is not: the page's blocks and the way past them are the top document's): "bypass blocks" is a whole-page concern, matching aria-hidden-body / page-title-present's pattern of evaluating the document directly rather than a scoped root. Not while a modal dialog is open: the rest of the page is inert then, so the scan sees the dialog, not the page. A custom element whose ElementInternals give it the main or heading role (this.attachInternals().role) counts as a <main> or a heading does.
expectation: At least one of the following recognized WCAG 2.4.1 techniques is present: (a) a main landmark (<main>, or an element whose role attribute resolves to main: the first real role token, in any case), ARIA11: a screen reader user can jump straight to it, bypassing everything before it (nav, header, repeated blocks) in one step; (b) a working skip link, technique G1: an <a href="#id"> (or legacy <a name="id">) whose name reads as a skip link in one of the shipped languages (helpers.hasSkipLinkWording, as skip-link uses) and whose target resolves to a real element in the link's own tree (light DOM or the same shadow root), outside any navigation or complementary landmark (<nav>, <aside>, or the role): a link to the menu or a sidebar skips to no main content. Not required to be positioned before a <nav> or be keyboard-focus-order-first; (c) at least one heading (<h1>-<h6>, or a role resolving to heading) that is both included in the accessibility tree AND visible (not off-screen, clipped, opacity:0, zero-size-overflow-hidden, or drawn wholly above the top of the page or left of its start, where no scrolling reaches), and outside any navigation or complementary landmark, technique H69: heading navigation is itself a standards-recognized bypass mechanism (e.g. a screen reader's "jump by heading" command), but ACT 047fe0's own Expectation requires visibility too, since a screen-reader-only heading leaves sighted keyboard users with no equivalent way to locate the start of non-repeated content. H69 puts headings at the start of each section of content: one inside the navigation heads the repeated block, and jumping to it skips nothing (ACT 047fe0, Failed Example 4).

examples.explanation: A main landmark exists, a recognized bypass mechanism.

title: <canvas> must provide a text alternative
description: Checks that <canvas> elements provide a text alternative via fallback content or an accessible name.
applicability: Applies to <canvas> elements included in the accessibility tree. Hidden elements are excluded whether or not they are focusable.
expectation:
Each applicable <canvas> provides a text alternative via fallback content or an accessible name, with two exceptions:

- role="img" (the first token of the role attribute that names a known role, matched case-insensitively) makes the canvas's children presentational and its name comes from the author only, so fallback content does not count: aria-labelledby, aria-label or title must name it.
- role="none"/"presentation" (resolved the same way) marks the canvas decorative, and it passes. The role is ignored (presentational role conflict) when the canvas is focusable or carries aria-label/aria-labelledby, and the canvas is then judged like any other.

examples.explanation: Fallback content between the tags provides a text alternative.
No fallback content and no accessible name.

title: <canvas> text alternative must be appropriate (manual review)
description: Flags <canvas> elements with a detected text alternative for human review of equivalence and appropriateness.
applicability: Applies to <canvas> elements that already carry a text alternative: fallback content inside the element, an ARIA name, or a title. A <canvas> with none of those has no alternative whose quality could be judged; that's canvas-text-alternative-present's failure. The element must be included in the accessibility tree, and role="presentation"/"none" takes it out of scope unless it is focusable, which restores its role.
expectation: Human review is required to confirm that the provided text alternative is accurate and appropriate.
reports:
- `reasonCode`: `TEXT_ALTERNATIVE_REVIEW`.
- `value`: the text alternative to review. When the fallback content has no text of its own but holds an image with alt text or an element with an aria-label, this is the placeholder `fallback-content`.
- `mechanism`: where the text alternative comes from: `canvas-fallback` (content inside the <canvas>), `aria-labelledby`, `aria-label` or `title`.
- `flags`: notes on how the text alternative was found, such as `title-used` when only the title attribute provides it.

examples.explanation: The fallback text "Bar chart" is present but generic — worth confirming it conveys the actual data, not just the chart type.
No fallback content, ARIA name, or title exists to review; that's `canvas-text-alternative-present`'s failure instead.

title: Click handlers on elements that are not native controls must work by keyboard
description: Checks that an element that is not a native control and has a click handler (an inline onclick, or a click listener the listener hook saw) can take keyboard focus and that a key handler on it, an ancestor or a descendant receives its keys, so a keyboard user can run what a click runs.
expectation:
A keyboard user can run what the click runs. Chromium fires `click` on Enter or Space for native controls only: a `<span role="button" tabindex="0" onclick>` gets focus but does nothing on either key.

- The element, or one of its flat-tree descendants, is in the tab order, and an inline key handler (`onkeydown`, `onkeyup`, `onkeypress`) is on it, an ancestor or a descendant, so key events from the focused element can reach one: pass.
- The element or a descendant is in the tab order, but no inline key handler is there: cantTell (`CLICK_HANDLER_NO_KEY_HANDLER`), check that Enter and Space do what a click does.
- The element or a descendant can take focus, but only with `tabindex="-1"`, and no ancestor has a key handler: cantTell (`CLICK_HANDLER_NOT_IN_TAB_ORDER`). Tab never reaches it; a script may move focus there, as a roving tabindex does.
- With the listener hook, a key listener added from script on the element or a descendant counts as an inline key handler does. One only on an ancestor, a shadow root the element is in, the document or the window may handle the element's keys or only others': cantTell (`CLICK_HANDLER_KEY_LISTENER_ABOVE`).
- The element is in the tab order, its role is button, link, checkbox, switch, tab, menuitem, menuitemcheckbox or menuitemradio, and a hook installed before the page's scripts saw no key listener on it, a descendant, an ancestor, a shadow root it is in, the document or the window, nor is an inline key handler there: fail (`CLICK_HANDLER_NO_KEY_LISTENER`). No key event reaches a handler, so Enter and Space do nothing. Unless a focus or focusin listener is on it, an ancestor, a shadow root it is in, the document or the window: it may add the key listener once the element has focus, or, for a tab, show its panel on focus, so cantTell (`CLICK_HANDLER_FOCUS_LISTENER`).
- Neither it nor a descendant can take focus, and its role is button, link, checkbox or switch: fail (`CLICK_HANDLER_CONTROL_NOT_FOCUSABLE`). The element says it is a control, and Tab never reaches it, as in WCAG failure F42 for scripted links. Unless an ancestor carries `aria-activedescendant` or an inline key handler, or is a focusable composite widget (grid, treegrid, listbox, menu, menubar, tree, tablist, toolbar, radiogroup, combobox), which may operate it without moving focus to it: then cantTell.
- Neither it nor a descendant can take focus, with another widget role or `cursor: pointer`: cantTell (`CLICK_HANDLER_NOT_FOCUSABLE`). An option of a combobox's list or a cell of a grid is often operated from the element that keeps focus, and the action may be offered by another control of the page.
reports:
- `role`: the element's ARIA role, or `''` for none.
- `focusable`: whether the element itself can take focus.

examples.explanation: The span takes focus and its key handler runs the same action as the click.
The element says it is a button and runs a click handler, but keyboard focus can never reach it.
The span takes focus, but Enter and Space fire no click on it and it has no inline key handler; a listener added from script would not show in the markup.

title: Comboboxes have an accessible name
description: Checks that elements with role="combobox" expose a non-empty accessible name.
applicability: Applies to elements whose role attribute resolves to combobox: its first token naming a known role, matched in any case, is combobox, so role="foo combobox" and role="COMBOBOX" count while role="link combobox" (a link) does not. The element must be included in the accessibility tree. An element with the matching implicit role but no role attribute is out of scope. A custom element whose ElementInternals give it the role (this.attachInternals().role), with no role attribute naming another, is in scope too: that is its default role, and no other rule checks it.
expectation: The element has a non-empty accessible name from aria-label, from an aria-labelledby that resolves to non-empty text, or from title. role="combobox" is name-from-author-only, so subtree text is never accepted: text sitting inside a custom combobox widget is not reliably exposed as its name. On a labelable element (<input role="combobox">) an associated <label> counts as well. On a text-like <input> or a <textarea>, the placeholder counts last (HTML-AAM's final name source): a placeholder-only label is a 3.3.2 question, not a missing name.

examples.explanation: `aria-label` names the combobox.
No accessible name from any supported mechanism.

title: Color contrast is computable for rendered text
description: Determines whether sufficient information is available to compute the color contrast for visible text (e.g., no gradients/images/blend modes that make background indeterminate).
applicability: Applies to every visible text node in scope, plus the label of <input type="button">/[type="submit"]/[type="reset"], which is rendered from the value attribute and so is invisible to a text-node walk, and the text a form field shows: the current value of a <textarea> or of an <input> that shows text (text, search, email, url, tel, password, number, the date and time types), or, while the value is empty, its placeholder, in the ::placeholder color, font, opacity and background (only where the browser computes that style; jsdom does not). The text of a drop-down <select> (no `multiple`, a size of 1 or none, not `appearance: base-select`) counts as the select's, drawn by the closed control in its colors, font and background: its shown option, and any other option with the select's colors. In a browser, so is the text a ::before or ::after `content` generates (strings, attr() as the browser resolves it, counters), and a list item's ::marker text (a number or a letter, or a string; a bullet or an image isn't text), each judged in the pseudo-element's color and font, on its element; jsdom computes no pseudo-element styles, so there it is left out. Text counts only when its element is DOM-visible under the run's visibility mode, is not clipped out of sight by the sr-only technique (clip or clip-path), and belongs neither to a disabled control nor to the label of one, WCAG's inactive-user-interface-component exception. Subtrees excluded via engineOptions.excludeSelectors are skipped, and open shadow roots are walked as roots in their own right.
expectation: Both sides of the contrast calculation can be established from CSS for every applicable text node: an effective background resolving to an opaque color, and a parsable foreground color. Where either cannot be, a background image or gradient (a gradient of one color is that color, and a layer that paints nothing under the text, such as a 1px underline, is left out), mix-blend-mode, a filter (other than drop-shadow() alone over an opaque background under all of the text, which hides the shadow) or backdrop-filter, a text-shadow (which may add contrast this engine has no glyph-rendering model to account for), a -webkit-text-stroke outline (drawn in its own color, often most of the glyph), a ::first-line or ::first-letter in a color of its own (which text it paints depends on line breaks), opacity on an ancestor, or on the text's own element over a background of its own, that can't be resolved against what lies behind it, a root background that never becomes opaque where the page's canvas can't be known (in a frame, under forced colors; elsewhere text is measured on the canvas, see contrast-minimum), a color that does not parse, or an option of a drop-down <select>, other than the shown one, with a color, background or opacity of its own (SELECT_OPTION_COLOR: it is shown only in the list the select opens, which the platform draws in those colors or in its own), or, in an emulator such as jsdom, a text color that can't be worked out in the color scheme the page is drawn in (COLOR_SCHEME_NOT_RENDERED), the result is cantTell naming the blocker. This rule is the one that reports that uncertainty, which is what lets contrast-minimum and contrast-enhanced stay silent on the same text instead of guessing at a ratio. One exception: text drawn by a stroke or a shadow, every color of which, its fill included when seen, is below the AA ratio against a flat background, fails contrast-minimum and contrast-enhanced, and is not asked about here.
reports:
- `blockerProperty`, `blockerValue` (a CSS effect in the way): the CSS property that blocks the calculation and its value, for example `mix-blend-mode`, `filter`, `text-shadow`, `-webkit-text-stroke` or `opacity`.
- `blockerSelector` (a CSS effect in the way): a selector for the element that has it, which may be an ancestor of the text.
- `backgroundFillType` (a background image or gradient): `image`, `gradient`, `imageAndGradient`, or `unknown`.
- `background`, `backgroundAlpha` (a background that never becomes opaque, or a color that does not parse): the background color as far as it could be worked out, as an `rgba()` string, and its opacity from 0 to 1.
- `eligibleTextCount` (the pass): how many text nodes were checked.
- `assumptionsCount`, `assumptionsApplied` (the pass): how many text nodes needed an assumption to get a background, and which ones were made. Each item is a code; `ROOT_CANVAS_FALLBACK` means a page background that never becomes opaque was taken to sit on the canvas color the scan names (`contrast.rootCanvasFallback`), or, with the `auditorAssist` mode where the page's own canvas can't be known (in a frame, under forced colors), on that color, white by default. Text measured on the canvas the page's color scheme gives it needs none.
- `generatedBy` (generated text that can't be measured): `::before`, `::after` or `::marker`, the pseudo-element whose text is asked about; the selector names its element. `GENERATED_TEXT_UNREADABLE` is content whose text can't be read (a counter in a style of the page's own), `GENERATED_TEXT_POSITIONED` a pseudo-element taken out of the flow with no opaque background of its own.
- `typography.fontSizePx`, `typography.fontSizePt` (each text asked about): the font size as drawn, in CSS pixels and in points, as contrast-minimum reports it: the computed size times CSS zoom, an SVG scale or font-size-adjust. `typography.declaredFontSizePx` and `typography.sizeScaledBy` where it is drawn at another size than its font-size.
- `typography.fontWeight`, `typography.fontWeightLabel`: the computed font weight as a number (400, 700) and as written.
- `typography.isBold`, `typography.isLargeText`: whether the text counts as bold (700 or more), and as large text by core's definition (24px, or 14pt and bold), the size that only needs 3:1. Generated text has its pseudo-element's font, at its computed size.
- The typography fields are a stable contract, as they are in contrast-minimum, unlike the rest of `data.details`.
- `forcedColors` (every occurrence, when the colors measured were forced): `true`, and the hint says to check the page again with forced colors off. A scan under forced colors measures the page's own colors, so this is there only where it could not keep the page in them.

examples.explanation: Foreground and background are both flat, opaque colors, so a ratio can be computed (whether or not it later passes AA/AAA).
A `background-image` behind the text is not a flat color, so no contrast ratio can be computed at all.

title: Text meets enhanced color contrast (AAA)
description: Checks that visible text has a contrast ratio of at least 7:1 (normal) or 4.5:1 (large), when contrast is computable from CSS.
applicability: Applies to the visible text contrast-computable applies to, see that rule for the eligibility gates, narrowed to text whose background and foreground are actually computable. Eligible text that is not computable leaves this rule notApplicable rather than cantTell: reporting that uncertainty belongs to contrast-computable, so the two never report the same text twice.
expectation: Every computable text node reaches the ratio SC 1.4.6 requires for its size: 4.5:1 for large text, 7:1 for everything else. Text is large at 24px or more, or at 14pt (about 18.667px) or more when the computed font weight is 700 or higher. Text drawn by a -webkit-text-stroke or a text-shadow is left to contrast-computable, except where every color it is drawn in, its fill among them unless the fill draws nothing (transparent, or the color of its background), is below the ratio against a flat background: no reading of it can then meet the criterion, and it fails, measured by the best of those colors (`drawnBy`: `textStroke` or `textShadow`). Margin (`contrast-ratio`): of the text that reaches its ratio, the element closest to it, with the ratio unrounded against the one its size requires; `context.largeText` says which. Only text within 10% of its ratio counts as close, so text further above it gives no margin. `measuredCount` counts the elements whose contrast was computed. Text part of which a ::first-line or ::first-letter paints in a color of its own is measured in both colors: where both reach their ratio it passes, where both fall short it fails (`pseudoElementColor` names the pseudo-element), and where they disagree it is left to contrast-computable. Text with no opaque background behind it, up to the root, is measured on the canvas the browser paints under the page, in the color scheme the page is drawn in, and, on a page that supports light and dark, in the other where its colors can't change with the scheme, as contrast-minimum describes. Normal-size text whose background can't be worked out still fails when its color can't reach 7:1 on any background (`CONTRAST_UNREACHABLE_ANY_BACKGROUND`, `metrics.bestRatio`: its ratio against white or black, whichever is higher). A field's placeholder below its ratio (`PLACEHOLDER_BELOW_THRESHOLD`) fails when the page chose its colors: the placeholder's color, opacity or background, or the field's background, differ from the browser's own, read in a blank frame. A placeholder left in the browser's own colors is taken to meet the ratio (WCAG G148), and when that can't be told it is a `cantTell` occurrence.
reports:
- `metrics.ratio` (a FAIL): the text's contrast ratio, for example 4.5 for 4.5:1, unrounded, against `metrics.threshold` (7, or 4.5 for large text).
- `colors.foregroundHex`, `colors.backgroundHex` (a FAIL): the text and background colors the ratio was computed from, as hex (the text in the -webkit-text-fill-color it is painted in, `color` unless set). A semi-transparent text color is first blended onto the background.
- `selectField` (a drop-down select in the browser's own background): `backgroundHex`, its computed background, and `fieldHex`, the Field color Chromium paints it in. The text is measured against both and the lower ratio is reported.
- `colors.foregroundRgba`, `colors.backgroundRgba` (a FAIL): the same colors as `rgba()` strings.
- `typography.fontSizePx`, `typography.fontSizePt` (a FAIL): the font size as drawn (the computed size times CSS zoom, or for SVG text its viewBox and transform scale, and times what font-size-adjust scales the font by), in CSS pixels and in points.
- `typography.declaredFontSizePx`, `typography.sizeScaledBy` (a FAIL drawn at another size): the computed font-size, and what drew it otherwise (`zoom`, `svg`, `font-size-adjust`). Where that puts the text on the other side of the large-text line, the hint says so (`contrast_hint_drawnSize`).
- `typography.fontWeight`, `typography.fontWeightLabel`, `typography.isBold` (a FAIL): the computed font weight as a number, `bold` (700 or more) or `normal`, and whether it counts as bold.
- `typography.isLargeText` (a FAIL): whether the text counts as large, which sets the threshold.
- The ratio, threshold and typography fields above are a stable contract, unlike the rest of `data.details`.
- `assumptionsApplied`, `assumedRootCanvasColor` (a FAIL): `null` unless the page background never became opaque and was taken to sit on a canvas color: one the scan names (`contrast.rootCanvasFallback`), or, with the `auditorAssist` mode where the page's own canvas can't be known (in a frame, under forced colors), the fallback. Then `assumptionsApplied` is `["ROOT_CANVAS_FALLBACK"]` and `assumedRootCanvasColor` is that color. Text on the canvas the page's color scheme gives it is measured on that canvas, with neither.
- `colorScheme` (a FAIL on the canvas of a page that supports light and dark): `'light'` or `'dark'`, the scheme in which the text falls short, where it passes in the other; absent where it falls short in every scheme measured.
- `colorSchemesChecked` (a FAIL, and the pass): the schemes the text on the canvas was measured in, where the page supports both and one could not be measured.
- `generatedBy` (a FAIL on generated text): `::before`, `::after` or `::marker`, the pseudo-element whose text is measured; the selector names its element, and the colors and font are the pseudo-element's.
- `eligibleTextCount`, `computableTextCount` (the pass, and the result's own `data.details` when it is notApplicable because no text was computable, which lists no occurrence): how many text nodes were in scope, and how many of those had colors that could be worked out. The pass repeats both under `metrics`.
- `forcedColors` (every occurrence, and that notApplicable result's details, when the colors measured were forced): `true`, and the hint says to check the page again with forced colors off. A scan under forced colors measures the page's own colors, so this is there only where it could not keep the page in them.
