Gray on white is about 4.6:1 — passes the AA minimum but fails the stricter 7:1 AAA threshold.

title: Text meets minimum color contrast (AA)
description: Checks that visible text has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 (normal) or 3:1 (large), when contrast is computable from CSS.
applicability: Applies to the visible text contrast-computable applies to, see that rule for the eligibility gates, narrowed to text whose background and foreground are actually computable. Eligible text that is not computable leaves this rule notApplicable rather than cantTell: reporting that uncertainty belongs to contrast-computable, so the two never report the same text twice.
expectation: Every computable text node reaches the ratio SC 1.4.3 requires for its size: 3:1 for large text, 4.5:1 for everything else. Text is large at 24px or more, or at 14pt (about 18.667px) or more when the computed font weight is 700 or higher. Text drawn by a -webkit-text-stroke or a text-shadow is left to contrast-computable, except where every color it is drawn in, its fill among them unless the fill draws nothing (transparent, or the color of its background), is below the ratio against a flat background: no reading of it can then meet the criterion, and it fails, measured by the best of those colors (`drawnBy`: `textStroke` or `textShadow`). Margin (`contrast-ratio`): of the text that reaches its ratio, the element closest to it, with the ratio unrounded against the one its size requires; `context.largeText` says which. Only text within 10% of its ratio counts as close, so text further above it gives no margin. `measuredCount` counts the elements whose contrast was computed. Text part of which a ::first-line or ::first-letter paints in a color of its own is measured in both colors: where both reach their ratio it passes, where both fall short it fails (`pseudoElementColor` names the pseudo-element), and where they disagree it is left to contrast-computable. contrast-computable decides what to ask about at WCAG's ratios. At ratios of this rule's own (a variant's settings), text in two colors that disagree only at those ratios, and text drawn by an outline or a shadow whose best color reaches them but not WCAG's AA ratio, are asked about here (`PSEUDO_ELEMENT_COLOR`, `TEXT_STROKE`, `TEXT_SHADOW`), since no other rule would. Text drawn by an outline whose best color lies between WCAG's AA ratio and a higher ratio of the variant's fails here and is asked about by contrast-computable too: two answers to two requirements, the variant's and WCAG 1.4.3. A field's placeholder below its ratio (`PLACEHOLDER_BELOW_THRESHOLD`) fails when the page chose its colors: the placeholder's color, opacity or background, or the field's background, differ from the browser's own, read in a blank frame. A placeholder left in the browser's own colors is taken to meet the ratio (WCAG G148), and when that can't be told it is a `cantTell` occurrence. Text with no opaque background behind it, up to the root, is measured on the canvas the browser paints under the page, in either contrast mode: the Canvas color of the color scheme the page is drawn in, which the page's own color-scheme (on the root, or in <meta name="color-scheme">) decides, as CSS Color Adjustment 1 defines it. A page that declares no scheme is drawn in light, on white, whatever the user prefers; one that declares only dark is drawn on the dark canvas. In a browser the colors are read from the page; an emulator (jsdom), which resolves no system color, takes Chromium's (#121212 for the dark canvas, #ffffff for the text a dark scheme gives). A canvas the scan names, when `contrast.rootCanvasFallback` gives one, is measured in its place. Where the canvas can't be known (in a frame, where the page around it may show through; under forced colors, where it is the user's palette) the text is left to contrast-computable, or measured on the fallback with the `auditorAssist` mode. A page that supports both schemes (`light dark`) is drawn in the one the user prefers. The scan sees that one (in a browser, as it is drawn; jsdom draws light), and its text is measured there and, where its colors can't change with the scheme, in the other too, on that scheme's canvas: not where a rule in a prefers-color-scheme query, a light-dark() value or a system color (other than the scheme's own text and link colors, where no rule colors the text) reaches the text's color or a background behind it. It fails where it fails in either scheme measured, and passes where it passes in each.
reports:
- `metrics.ratio` (text below the threshold): the text's contrast ratio against its background (4.5 for 4.5:1), against `metrics.threshold`, the ratio its size requires.
- `colors.foregroundHex`, `colors.backgroundHex` (text below the threshold): the text color (the -webkit-text-fill-color it is painted in, `color` unless set) and the background color behind it, as hex, after any transparency is blended in. `colors.foregroundRgba` and `colors.backgroundRgba` give the same two colors in `rgba()` form.
- `selectField` (a drop-down select in the browser's own background): `backgroundHex`, its computed background, and `fieldHex`, the Field color Chromium paints it in. The text is measured against both and the lower ratio is reported.
- `typography.fontSizePx`, `typography.fontSizePt` (text below the threshold): the font size as drawn, in CSS pixels and in points: the computed size times CSS zoom, or for SVG text its viewBox and transform scale, and times what font-size-adjust scales the font by (its adjust value over the font's own aspect, read in a browser). This is the size the large-text threshold is judged on, as WCAG's "size when the content is delivered".
- `typography.declaredFontSizePx`, `typography.sizeScaledBy` (text below the threshold, drawn at another size): the computed font-size, and what drew it otherwise (`zoom`, `svg`, `font-size-adjust`). Where that puts the text on the other side of the large-text line, the hint says so (`contrast_hint_drawnSize`).
- `typography.fontWeight`, `typography.fontWeightLabel` (text below the threshold): the computed font weight as a number (400, 700) and as written.
- `typography.isBold`, `typography.isLargeText` (text below the threshold): whether the text counts as bold, and as large text, the size that only needs 3:1.
- The ratio, threshold and typography fields above are a stable contract, unlike the rest of `data.details`.
- `assumptionsApplied`, `assumedRootCanvasColor` (text below the threshold): `null` unless the page sets no opaque background and the text was measured on a canvas color the scan names (`contrast.rootCanvasFallback`), or, with the `auditorAssist` mode where the page's own canvas can't be known (in a frame, under forced colors), on the fallback (white by default). Then `assumptionsApplied` is `['ROOT_CANVAS_FALLBACK']` and `assumedRootCanvasColor` is that color.
- `colorScheme` (text below the threshold, on the canvas of a page that supports light and dark): `'light'` or `'dark'`, the scheme in which it falls short, where it passes in the other, and the hint names it; the ratio and colors are that scheme's. Absent where it falls short in every scheme measured (then reported in the scheme the page is drawn in) and on a page with one scheme.
- `colorSchemesChecked` (text below the threshold, and the pass): the schemes the text on the canvas was measured in, `['light']` or `['dark']`, where the page supports both and one could not be measured. A binding can scan again with the browser in the other scheme. Absent where every scheme the page supports was measured.
- `generatedBy` (generated text below the threshold): `::before`, `::after` or `::marker`, the pseudo-element whose text is measured; the selector names its element, and the colors and font are the pseudo-element's.
- `eligibleTextCount`, `computableTextCount` (the pass, and the result's own `data.details` when it is notApplicable because no text was computable, which lists no occurrence): how many text nodes the rule looked at, and how many of them had colors it could compute. Repeated under `metrics` on a pass.
- `forcedColors` (every occurrence, and that notApplicable result's details, when the colors measured were forced): `true`, and the hint says to check the page again with forced colors off. A scan under forced colors measures the page's own colors, so this is there only where it could not keep the page in them.

50% ancestor (group) opacity over white composites to a flat gray around 4:1, below the AA minimum.

title: A button or link should not take its name only from its title
description: Flags a button or link whose only accessible name is its title attribute, shown only on mouse hover, for manual review.
applicability: Buttons and links in the accessibility tree with a non-empty `title` attribute: `<a href>`, `<area href>`, `<button>`, `<input>` of type `button`, `submit`, `reset` or `image`, and elements whose role attribute, or ElementInternals, give them the button or link role.
expectation:
Accessible Name Computation takes a title as the name only when nothing else names the element: author naming (`aria-labelledby`, `aria-label`), an image button's `alt`, an input button's `value`, or, for buttons and links, their content.

- Something other than the title names the control: pass. The title is its description, a tooltip.
- The title is its only name: cantTell (`NAME_FROM_TITLE_ONLY`).

The name is valid, so 4.1.2 is met, but a title is shown only on mouse hover: not on touch screens, not when the control takes focus from the keyboard, and not as text a person using speech input can read and say. Check whether the control can be given visible text, or an `aria-label` when it shows only an icon, with the title kept as a tooltip if wanted.
reports: - `role`: the control's role, `button` or `link`.

examples.explanation: The button's text names it; the `title` is a tooltip.
The `title` is the button's only name, shown only on mouse hover. A person checks whether it can have visible text, or an `aria-label`.

title: Focus indicator must not be removed without a replacement
description: Flags elements in the tab order whose focus outline is removed, by a :focus/:focus-visible rule or by a rule with no state such as a { outline: none }, with no replacement indicator (border, box-shadow, background, ...) in any focus rule matching them.
applicability: Elements in sequential focus navigation (tabbable and rendered) on a page whose accessible stylesheets contain at least one rule that removes the outline. With no such rule anywhere, every element keeps the user agent's own indicator and there is nothing to check.
expectation: No element is matched by a rule that removes the outline (`outline: none`, `outline: 0`, `outline-color: transparent`, ...) unless some focus rule matching it draws a replacement: a border, box-shadow, background, color change, a positive outline of its own, or a `::before`/`::after` decoration. The removing rule is either a `:focus`/`:focus-visible` rule, or a rule with no state at all (`a { outline: none }`, `* { outline: 0 }`): an author declaration outranks the user agent's focus outline whatever its specificity, so it removes the indicator in the focused state too (WCAG F78). A rule that removes it only under `:not(:focus-visible)` keeps it for keyboard focus and is not counted; nor is the focus-visible polyfill's form of it, `:not(.focus-visible)` under `.js-focus-visible`, or `:not([data-focus-visible-added])` under `[data-js-focus-visible]`.
reports:
- `suppressingSelectors`: the selector of each style sheet rule that removes the element's outline, one item per selector.
- `styleSheet` or `styleElementIndex`: when those rules are all in one style sheet, its href as written, or the position of its <style> element among the page's, from 1.

examples.explanation: `:focus { outline: none; }` removes the focus indicator, and no other rule matching this link draws a replacement.
A rule with no `:focus` still applies while the link has focus, and it outranks the browser's own focus outline (F78). No focus rule draws a replacement.

examples.html:
<style>.reset-shadow:focus { outline: none; box-shadow: 0 0 0 3px navy; }</style>
<button class="reset-shadow" type="button">Send</button>
examples.explanation: The same rule that removes the outline draws a `box-shadow` in its place.

title: Focusable elements must not be visually hidden
description: Checks that keyboard-focusable elements are not visually hidden by CSS techniques that can leave them in the tab order.
applicability: Applies to elements that are tabbable (keyboard-focusable) but are visually hidden via CSS techniques that can leave them in the tab order.
expectation: No element should be tabbable while visually hidden (e.g., opacity:0, clipped, off-screen). An element that CSS brings back into view when it takes focus is not hidden while focused, and is not flagged: the usual skip-link pattern (`.skip { position: absolute; left: -9999px } .skip:focus { left: 0 }`), or a hiding rule that stops applying on focus (`.visually-hidden-focusable:not(:focus) { clip: rect(0 0 0 0) }`). A focus rule nested in another (`.skip { &:focus { top: 0 } }`) counts as written out; one whose focus is inside `:has()` counts, for its subject, as `:focus-within` does. A focus rule that isn't `!important` doesn't override an `!important` declaration that hides the element.
reports:
- `metrics.visibilityHints`: how the element is hidden while it can take focus: `opacityZero`, `offscreen`, `clipped` or `zeroSizeOverflowHidden` (no size, with overflow hidden) by its own styles; when they show it, `outOfReach` (a container is positioned off screen, or is fixed and clips its content where its px lengths put it wholly outside the viewport, or, in a browser, the box focus would show lies where no scrolling reaches) or `containerClipped` (a container is clipped to nothing, has no size with overflow hidden, or is scaled to nothing, or, in a browser, the element lies wholly outside a container with `overflow: clip`, which focus doesn't scroll).
- `runtimeProbe`: `null` unless focusing the element moved focus straight to another element (`cssHiddenTabbable_runtimeRedirect_needsReview`). Then it holds `redirected: true` and the tag and id of the element focus moved to (`redirectedToTag`, `redirectedToId`). Only the first three hidden elements are tried this way.

examples.explanation: The link stays in the tab order despite `opacity:0` making it invisible to sighted keyboard users.
The link is both focusable and visible — nothing to flag.

examples.html: Skip to content
examples.explanation: The link is off-screen at rest, but its `:focus` rule brings it back into view when it takes focus.

title: CSS must not lock the page to a single orientation
description: Checks that no @media (orientation: portrait|landscape) rule sets a transform: rotate(...) on the page, a known technique for defeating device orientation, and asks about any such rule that hides the page's main content.
applicability: Any accessible (same-document, non-cross-origin) stylesheet, inline `<style>` blocks and same-origin `<link>` stylesheets already loaded into `document.styleSheets`, sheets adopted by the document, and those of each open shadow root, whose rules are matched against that root's elements.
expectation: No `@media (orientation: portrait)` or `@media (orientation: landscape)` block sets a `transform`/`-webkit-transform`/`rotate` rotation of approximately 90 degrees (mod 180, i.e. ~90 or ~270), the well-known technique for visually forcing one orientation regardless of the device's actual orientation, which defeats WCAG 1.3.4's requirement that content not restrict its view to a single display orientation unless that orientation is essential. Such a rotation is judged on the visible elements its selector matches (ACT b33eff), visibility judged without the rotation itself: it fails where one of them holds the page's content (as defined below for hidden content), and any other element turned that way is asked about (cantTell): an arrow pointing to a panel beside it in one orientation and below it in the other locks nothing. A rule that turns no visible element, or only a pseudo-element, has nothing to judge. A second shape is asked about (cantTell): an orientation media block that hides the page's content with `display: none` or `visibility: hidden`, the usual form of WCAG F100 (content replaced by a "rotate your device" message in one orientation). The hidden element counts as the page's content when it is `html` or `body`, the `main` landmark, an ancestor of it, or, on a page without a main landmark, an element holding at least half of the body's text. Where the page has no <main> and no role="main", a custom element whose ElementInternals give it the main role (this.attachInternals().role) is the main landmark. Whether the orientation is essential, and whether the page stays usable, is left to a person.
reports:
- `mediaText` (a rotation or hidden content): the media query that holds the rule, such as `(orientation: portrait)`. A rotation of an element that doesn't hold the page's content is reported against that element (ORIENTATION_MEDIA_ROTATES_ELEMENT).
- `selectorText` (a rotation or hidden content): the selector of the style rule that rotates or hides. Empty when it could not be read.
- `unreadableSheetCount` (`STYLESHEETS_NOT_READABLE`): how many style sheets could not be read, usually because they come from another origin.

examples.explanation: No orientation media query rotates the page.
A landscape media query forces a 90-degree rotation, locking the page to portrait regardless of device orientation.

title: Description lists must be structured correctly
description: Checks that <dl> elements only directly contain <dt>/<dd> groups (optionally wrapped in one <div>), <script>, <template>, or <style>.
applicability: Applies to <dl> elements that have at least one direct element child or non-whitespace text directly inside them.
expectation: Every direct element child is <dt>, <dd>, <script>, <template>, <style>, or a <div> whose own children are drawn from that same set (a single level of wrapping div is allowed, matching how authors commonly group dt/dd pairs). Non-whitespace text directly inside the <dl> or a wrapping <div> is an invalid child too. If the flattened set contains any <dt> or <dd> at all, it must contain BOTH (an unbalanced dt-without-dd or dd-without-dt is invalid), and read in order it must be groups of one or more <dt> followed by one or more <dd>: a <dd> before the first <dt> has no term, and a <dt> after the last <dd> has no definition. A flattened set with neither (an empty list, or one holding only <script>, <template> or <style>) is not a violation: the pairing is required only of a list that has items. Any other direct or wrapped child breaks the description-list semantics assistive technologies rely on. Every finding is reported at CANTTELL, not FAIL. HTML-AAM gives <dt> and <dd> their term and definition roles wherever they sit, so what a broken content model loses is the pairing of terms with definitions, which only the <dl>'s structure and order state. That is a WCAG failure (SC 1.3.1) only where the page shows the pairing, and H40 is only a sufficient technique: a person settles it.
reports: - `invalidChildren`: the children that do not belong in the list, one tag name per child (`#text` for text placed directly inside). Empty when the problem is a missing or misordered `<dt>`/`<dd>`.

examples.explanation: `<dl>`'s only direct children are `dt`/`dd`.

The `

` is a direct child of `

` that isn't `dt`/`dd` (or an allowed wrapper). The term and definition keep their roles, so whether a WCAG criterion fails depends on whether the page shows a pairing the markup breaks.

title: Scrolling <marquee> content must be possible to pause, stop, or hide
description: Asks, for each obsolete <marquee> element, whether the page offers a way to pause, stop, or hide its auto-scrolling content, since the element itself has none.
applicability: Applies to any scan scope; whether it contains a <marquee> element is always an answerable question. <marquee> is an obsolete, non-standard HTML element that browsers still render as auto-scrolling text, with no built-in user mechanism to pause, stop, or hide it.
expectation: Each <marquee> is reported as cantTell: the scrolling itself is certain, but a page can offer its own pause or stop control (a button calling the element's stop() method, for example), and then failure F16 does not apply. Whether such a control exists is for a person to check. A scope with no <marquee> passes; there is no separate not-applicable case.

examples.explanation: No `<marquee>` anywhere, which satisfies the rule outright; there is no separate not-applicable case. `<blink>` is not reported, since no browser makes it blink.
`<marquee>` scrolls its content and gives the user no way to pause, stop, or hide it; whether the page adds its own control is for a person to check. This rule never fails.

title: Dialogs have an accessible name
description: Checks that dialogs (elements with role="dialog" or role="alertdialog", and native <dialog> elements) expose a non-empty accessible name.
applicability: Applies to elements included in the accessibility tree whose role is dialog or alertdialog: an element whose role attribute resolves to one of those roles (the first token that names a concrete ARIA role wins, so role="alertdialog dialog" is an alertdialog), and a native <dialog> whose role attribute is absent or names no concrete role (its implicit role is dialog). A closed <dialog> is hidden and so not in scope. A custom element whose ElementInternals give it one of those roles (this.attachInternals().role), with no role attribute naming another, counts as a native element with that role does.
expectation: The element has a non-empty accessible name from aria-label, from an aria-labelledby that resolves to non-empty text, or from title. Both roles are name-from-author-only, so the heading or body text inside the dialog is not accepted as its name unless aria-labelledby points at it. A missing name is reported at CANTTELL, not FAIL. WAI-ARIA requires it ("Authors MUST provide an accessible name for a dialog"), but a dialog is not itself a user interface component in WCAG's sense, "a single control for a distinct function": its controls are, and each is named by its own rule. So the missing name proves the WAI-ARIA violation, not a failure of SC 4.1.2. It can still be a WCAG failure where the dialog shows a visible title that is not tied to it (that relationship is then not programmatically determinable, SC 1.3.1); a person settles that.

examples.explanation: `aria-label` names the dialog.

No accessible name, which WAI-ARIA requires; visible body text doesn't count toward a dialog's name. A dialog is not a single control, so whether a WCAG criterion fails depends on whether it shows a title that is not tied to it.

title: Description-list items must be inside a description list
description: Checks that <dt>/<dd> elements are contained by a <dl>, directly or via one wrapping <div>.
applicability: Applies to <dt>/<dd> elements that have a parent element in the flat tree, as the page renders it: a <dt>/<dd> slotted into a shadow <dl><slot></slot></dl> is in that list, and a <slot> in between is seen through. A <dt>/<dd> a shadow host doesn't slot is not rendered and is left out.
expectation: The parent is <dl>, or the parent is a <div> whose own parent is <dl> (a single level of wrapping div is allowed, matching how authors commonly group dt/dd pairs). A <dt>/<dd> used outside a real description-list container keeps its term or definition role, but no list pairs it with the definition or term that goes with it. Every finding is reported at CANTTELL, not FAIL. HTML-AAM gives <dt> and <dd> their term and definition roles wherever they sit, so what a broken content model loses is the pairing of terms with definitions, which only the <dl>'s structure and order state. That is a WCAG failure (SC 1.3.1) only where the page shows the pairing, and H40 is only a sufficient technique: a person settles it.
reports: - `parentElement`: the tag name of the element's parent, the container it is in instead of a `<dl>`.

examples.explanation: Both `dt` and `dd` are inside a `<dl>` ancestor.
`<dt>` has no `<dl>` ancestor at all. It keeps its term role, so whether a WCAG criterion fails depends on whether the page shows it paired with a definition.

title: IDs must be unique
description: Checks that every non-empty id attribute value is unique within its own document or shadow tree.
applicability: Applies to any element carrying a non-empty id attribute. Visibility is irrelevant. A duplicate id breaks the same lookups whether the element renders or not, which is why ACT 3ea0c8 evaluates hidden elements too.
expectation: No other element in the same tree carries the same id value, compared exactly as written (id="a " and id="a" are different ids). Ids are scoped per document tree and per shadow tree, so the same id inside two different shadow roots is not a duplicate.
reports:
- `reasonCode`: `DUPLICATE_ID_IN_SHADOW_TREE` when the elements are in one shadow tree, which script builds and the page's served markup does not hold; `DUPLICATE_ID` otherwise. Both fail the same way.
- `id`: the duplicated id.
- `count`: how many elements in the same tree carry it.

examples.explanation: Each element has a distinct id.
The id `section-1` is used by two elements in the same tree, breaking `<label for>`, fragment links, and `getElementById`.

title: IDs referenced by ARIA must be unique
description: Checks that any id value referenced by an ARIA ID-reference attribute (aria-labelledby, aria-describedby, aria-owns, aria-controls, aria-activedescendant, aria-flowto, aria-errormessage, aria-details) is unique in the document.
applicability: Applies when the document contains at least one non-empty aria-labelledby, aria-describedby, aria-owns, aria-controls, aria-activedescendant, aria-flowto, aria-errormessage, or aria-details attribute (i.e. at least one ARIA ID reference exists to resolve).
expectation: For every id value referenced by one of those attributes, exactly one element in the document carries that id. A duplicate does not break the reference: it resolves to the first element in tree order, so the name is still computed. Whether that element is the intended target depends on author intent, which markup does not carry, so the outcome is cantTell.
reports:
- `id`: the duplicated id an ARIA attribute refers to.
- `duplicateCount`: how many elements in the document carry that id.

examples.explanation: The id `lbl` is unique, so the reference resolves unambiguously.
`aria-labelledby="lbl"` resolves to the first element with that id — whether that's the intended target is an authoring question the markup can't answer.

title: <embed> must provide a text alternative
description: Checks that <embed> elements provide a text alternative via an accessible name.
applicability: Applies to <embed> elements that are exposed to assistive technologies. Elements otherwise hidden from the accessibility tree remain applicable if they are tabbable or referenced by IDREF relationships (per engine eligibility checks). role="presentation"/role="none" are excluded only when not focusable.
expectation:
Each applicable <embed> provides a text alternative via:

- an accessible name (aria-labelledby/aria-label), OR
- a title attribute (best-effort fallback).

Note: <embed> does not support fallback content in HTML, so this rule does not check children.

examples.explanation: `aria-label` gives the embed an accessible name.
No accessible name and no fallback content.

title: <embed> text alternative must be appropriate (manual review)
description: Flags <embed> elements with a detected name for human review of appropriateness.
applicability: Applies to <embed> elements that already carry a text alternative: a non-empty aria-label, an aria-labelledby that resolves to non-empty text, or a non-empty title. An aria-labelledby pointing at a missing id resolves to nothing and so is not a text alternative to review; that element is embed-text-alternative-present's failure. The element must be included in the accessibility tree, and role="presentation"/"none" takes it out of scope unless it is focusable, which restores its role.
expectation: Human review is required to confirm that the provided text alternative is accurate and appropriate.
reports:
- `reasonCode`: `TEXT_ALTERNATIVE_REVIEW`.
- `ariaLabel`, `title`: the element's `aria-label` and `title`, or null when it has none.
- `ariaLabelledBy`: the ids in the element's `aria-labelledby`, or null when it has none.
- `ariaLabelledByText`: the text those ids point at, or null. Only looked up when the element has no `aria-label`, since `aria-label` then gives the name.

examples.explanation: A `title` is present — worth confirming it identifies the document well enough for someone who can't see the embedded viewer.
No aria-label, resolved aria-labelledby, or title exists to review; that's `embed-text-alternative-present`'s failure instead.

title: Headings must not be empty
description: Checks that heading elements (<h1>-<h6> or role="heading") have a non-empty accessible name.
applicability: Applies to elements with a heading role: native <h1>-<h6>, or any element whose role attribute resolves to heading (the first token naming a known role, matched case-insensitively, so role="foo heading" counts). A native heading keeps its role when no token is a known role, and loses it to any other resolved role. A native <hx> marked role="none" or "presentation" is still a heading when it can take focus or carries a global ARIA attribute, as WAI-ARIA's presentational roles conflict resolution has browsers ignore that role then. A custom element whose ElementInternals give it the heading role (this.attachInternals().role), with no role attribute naming another, counts as a native element with that role does.
expectation: The heading has a non-empty accessible name: aria-label, aria-labelledby, visible text content not hidden from assistive technology, or (as a last resort) a title attribute. An empty heading is announced as "heading, level N" with nothing else, which is confusing when navigating by heading. Reported at FAIL although no WCAG criterion is claimed: an empty heading is itself the barrier, as the ACT rule ffd0e9 treats it. A heading whose name may come from content no script can read (a closed shadow root, content nested too deep, a custom element naming itself through ElementInternals) is asked about instead, as the *-name-present rules do.

examples.explanation: The heading has visible text content.
The heading has no accessible name at all — nothing for a screen reader to announce.

title: Table header cells must not be empty
description: Checks that table header cells (<th>, or any element with role="columnheader"/"rowheader") have visible text content. A header named only via aria-label/aria-labelledby is also flagged, since real screen-reader/browser support for that is inconsistent.
applicability: Applies to <th> elements that don't carry a conflicting explicit role, plus any element (native <th> or not) whose role resolves to columnheader or rowheader. The role attribute is a fallback list: its first known, non-abstract token, in any case, is the role, so role="foo columnheader" counts, and a <th role="foo"> (no known token) keeps its implicit header role. A <th> that explicitly restates role="columnheader"/"rowheader" is still covered, but a <th role="presentation"> (no longer meaningfully a header) is correctly excluded, and an ARIA-role-only header (e.g. a <div role="columnheader"> in a role="grid"/role="table" widget) is caught too. A custom element whose ElementInternals give it the columnheader or rowheader role (this.attachInternals().role), with no role attribute naming another, counts as a native element with that role does.
expectation: The header cell has visible text content. A <th> named only via aria-label/aria-labelledby (no visible text) is ALSO flagged, not treated as equivalent: aria-label support on <th> is inconsistent in practice. NVDA+Firefox and iOS VoiceOver+Safari ignore it entirely (only visible text is announced), JAWS+Chrome/IE11 also only announce visible text in the header cell itself. Visible text is the one mechanism confirmed to work across every tested combination. See https://html5accessibility.com/stuff/2024/05/22/not-so-short-note-on-aria-label-usage-big-table-edition/.
reports: - `ariaName` (`TABLE_HEADER_NAME_NOT_VISIBLE_TEXT`): the name the header cell gets from `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` instead of visible text.

examples.explanation: The header cell has visible text content.
The header cell has no text content and no accessible name.

title: No part of a focused element should be hidden
description: Checks that no element in the tab order can take focus with any part of it hidden behind content the page keeps in place, such as a sticky header or footer or a cookie banner.
applicability: What focus-not-obscured-minimum applies to: in a browser, the elements in the tab order that are drawn and scroll with the page, and the `position: fixed` or `sticky` boxes that draw something over it. Without a layout (jsdom), notApplicable.
expectation: No element in the tab order can take focus with any part of it hidden behind such a box, even one it shows through (a semi-transparent or dimming box obscures it, as WCAG's Understanding 2.4.12 says, where focus-not-obscured-minimum lets it pass): where a box covers part of the window the page's `scroll-padding` doesn't take out, an element that reaches under it and can be scrolled there takes focus partly hidden. One finding per box, naming how many elements it can hide entirely and how many in part. A `scroll-padding` on the page at least as large as the box (C43) clears it. Content the user opened and can close without moving focus is allowed, and a script-made modal dialog that leaves the page able to take focus is reported apart, as in focus-not-obscured-minimum. It is focus-not-obscured-minimum run with `obscured: 'partly'` (a variant: docs/RULE_AUTHORING.md, "Rule variants"), so a fix to that rule's measuring reaches this one.
reports: - As focus-not-obscured-minimum's, with `metrics.partlyCount`: how many elements can take focus partly hidden, and not entirely.

title: A focused element must not be entirely hidden
description: Checks that no element in the tab order can take focus entirely hidden behind content the page keeps in place, such as a sticky header or footer or a cookie banner.
applicability: Applies, in a browser, to the elements in the tab order that are drawn and scroll with the page, and to the boxes the page keeps in place over it: `position: fixed` or `sticky` boxes that draw something (a background, an image or a picture), such as a sticky header or footer, a cookie banner or a chat widget. Without a layout (jsdom) nothing can be measured, and the rule is notApplicable.
expectation: No element in the tab order can take focus entirely hidden behind such a box. A browser scrolls a focused element into view only when it is not already in view, and counts as in view the whole window less the page's `scroll-padding`. So where a fixed or sticky box covers part of the window that `scroll-padding` doesn't take out, an element that fits under it and can be scrolled there takes focus there and stays hidden: as the user tabs down a page, the next link is often already in the strip a footer covers. The rule works out, for each box, which elements can end up entirely under it, then scrolls a few of them there and checks that the box is what the browser draws on top of them, and puts the page back where it was. A sticky box counts only for the elements in its containing block, where it can be. A box hides an element entirely only where it is drawn opaque: under a semi-transparent or dimming box (an `opacity` under 1 on it or a container, or a background color that isn't opaque) the element shows through, so it is not entirely hidden, as WCAG's Understanding 2.4.11 says; 2.4.12 counts it as obscured. One finding per box, naming how many elements it can hide and one of them. A page lists at most 50 boxes, in document order, and checks at most 150 elements; when boxes are left unchecked, the result's own `data.details` says how many boxes could hide an element (`boxCount`), how many are listed (`reportedCount`, at most `maxOccurrences`), how many weren't checked (`uncheckedCount`), and `truncated`. A `scroll-padding` on the page at least as large as the box (technique C43) clears it. Content the user opened and can close without moving focus, such as a chat panel closed with Escape, is allowed to cover the focused element (the criterion's second note); the rule can't tell who opened a box, so it asks. A script-made modal dialog (`aria-modal="true"`) that leaves the page behind it able to take focus is reported apart: focus can then reach elements its backdrop covers. A `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()` makes the page inert, so nothing behind it takes focus. It is the base of focus-not-obscured-enhanced (2.4.12), which asks about an element any part of which can be hidden (`obscured: 'partly'`).
reports:
- `metrics.entirelyCount`: how many elements in the tab order can take focus entirely hidden behind the box.
- `metrics.partlyCount`: with `obscured: 'partly'`, how many can take focus partly hidden, and not entirely.
- `metrics.position`: `fixed` or `sticky`, the box's own or that of the box it is drawn in.
- `metrics.side`: where the box sits, `top`, `bottom` or `middle`, for the `scroll-padding` that would clear it.
- `metrics.coverPx`: the height of the window the box covers that the page still counts as in view, in CSS pixels.
- `metrics.scrollPaddingPx`: the page's `scroll-padding` on that side.
- `metrics.paddingNeededPx`: the `scroll-padding` on that side that would clear the box, from that edge of the window to the box's far side (a box stacked under another counts both).
- `openedByUser`: whether a control marked expanded (`aria-expanded="true"`) names the box, or something in or around it, with `aria-controls`: content the user opened, which may cover the focused element if it closes without moving focus.
- `examples`: up to 5 of the elements it can hide, each `{ tag, text }`.
- `confirmedBy`: the element the rule scrolled under the box to check that the box is drawn on top of it, as `{ tag, text }`.

title: A script must not remove focus from an element as it receives it
description: Fails elements in the tab order whose inline onfocus handler only calls blur() on them, and asks about other handlers that call blur(), or focus() on another element, which can remove focus as soon as the element receives it.
applicability: Elements that can take focus, that the page renders, and whose inline `onfocus` handler calls `blur()`, or `focus()` on another element. Without such an element, or in a document where none can take focus, nothing is applicable.
expectation:
WCAG failure F55: a script that removes focus from an element when it receives it leaves a keyboard user unable to reach or operate it, and unable to see where focus is.

- `FOCUS_HANDLER_BLURS_SELF`: fail, on an element in the tab order, when the handler does only that (`this.blur()`, `blur()`, or `blur()` on `event.target` or `event.currentTarget`, by name or in brackets, possibly behind `if (this.blur)`, with at most a `return`), as F55's examples do. Focus goes nowhere: it is dropped, not sent elsewhere. Outside the tab order (tabindex="-1"), where a keyboard user doesn't reach it, it is asked about.

Each other element is asked about (cantTell):

- `FOCUS_HANDLER_CALLS_BLUR` when it calls `blur()` among other code, or on another element, where whether focus is lost depends on the script;
- `FOCUS_HANDLER_MOVES_FOCUS` when it calls `focus()` on another element (`document.body.focus()`), which takes focus away as it arrives, as F55's test checks.

A handler that sends focus somewhere (a focus-trap sentinel, a redirect) is the moves case and is asked about, never failed: the rule reads the handler's text, not what the page does, and a person can confirm it by tabbing to the element.
reports:
- `reasonCode`: `FOCUS_HANDLER_BLURS_SELF`, `FOCUS_HANDLER_CALLS_BLUR` or `FOCUS_HANDLER_MOVES_FOCUS`.
- `handler`: the onfocus attribute's value, whitespace collapsed, up to 120 characters; a longer one is cut and ends in `…`.
- `tabbable`: whether the element is in the tab order. One that is not can still receive focus from a click or a script.

examples.explanation: The link removes focus from itself as soon as it receives it, WCAG failure F55's own example: a keyboard user can't stay on it to follow it.
The handler calls `blur()` among other code, so whether focus is lost depends on the script.
The `<span>` cannot take focus, so its handler never runs.

title: Elements added to the tab order should have interactive semantics
description: Flags elements with tabindex >= 0 whose explicit role is a non-interactive structural/document role (e.g. heading, list, note, presentation), for manual review.
applicability: Elements with an explicit `tabindex` of `0` or greater (in the tab order) AND an explicit `role` attribute that resolves to one of a curated set of clearly non-interactive, structural/document roles. The attribute is a fallback list: its first known, non-abstract token, in any case, is the role (role="foo HEADING" is a heading, role="foo" is no role).
expectation: An element placed in the tab order on purpose should communicate why it's focusable: a role like `heading`, `list`, `note`, or `presentation` gives assistive technology no interactive semantic to announce, which is confusing for keyboard users who land on it and get no indication of what activating it (if anything) would do.
reports:
- `tabindex`: the element's `tabindex`, as a number (0 or greater).
- `role`: the non-interactive role the element carries.

examples.explanation: A heading role has no interactive behavior, so making it tabbable is unusual and worth a look.
`role="button"` is an interactive role, so being tabbable is expected.

title: Form field labels should be descriptive and distinguishable
description: Flags a visible form-field label that is a placeholder ("Label", "Field"), or that repeats another field's label with no visible context (heading, legend, or row) telling the two apart. English placeholders are always recognized, and German, Spanish, French or Japanese ones when the field is in that language.
applicability: Visible form fields: native `input` (excluding hidden and the button-like types), `select`, `textarea`, or an element with one of the ARIA widget roles ACT cc0f0a lists (checkbox, combobox, listbox, menuitemcheckbox, menuitemradio, radio, searchbox, slider, spinbutton, switch, textbox; the first real role token of the role attribute, in any case) that carry a visible programmatic label: a `<label>` association, or the elements `aria-labelledby` points at. A field named only by `aria-label`/`title` has no visible label to judge and is out of scope here (its labelling mechanism is `form-control-programmatic-label-quality`'s concern, its presence `form-control-programmatic-label-present`'s). A custom element whose ElementInternals give it one of those roles (this.attachInternals().role), with no role attribute naming another, counts as a native element with that role does. Finding nothing to ask about, it reports notApplicable, not pass: it applies only to what its check flags, and finding nothing there doesn't show that all is well.
expectation: The visible label text (a) is not a placeholder left in the markup ("label", "field", "enter text", ...), (b) is not shared with another field that no visible context tells apart (the same "Name" twice, with nothing visible on screen saying which is shipping and which is billing), and (c) is the whole of the field's programmatic label, not the visible fragment of a label whose descriptive part is hidden.
reports:
- `label`: the visible label text of the field.
- `sharedWithFields`: on `DUPLICATE_LABEL_TEXT`, the first three of those other fields, as the message names them (`#last (name="last")`).
- `sharedWith`: how many other fields have the same label with nothing visible telling them apart, a count. 0 when no other field shares it.
- `hiddenLabelParts`: how many parts of the field's label are hidden from sight, a count. 0 when the whole label is visible.

examples.explanation: The label text is the placeholder word "Label" itself, not a real description of the field.
The label text is a genuine, descriptive name for the field.

title: Form controls must have a programmatic label
description: Checks that form controls have a programmatic label via <label>, aria-label, aria-labelledby, title, or placeholder.
applicability: Applies to <input>, <select> and <textarea> elements included in the accessibility tree, excluding the input types hidden, submit, reset, button and image, which take their name from a value or alt attribute rather than from a label. A control whose role attribute resolves (first token naming a known role, case-insensitively) to an explicit ARIA widget role is out of scope, button, checkbox, combobox, listbox, textbox, slider and the rest of ROLE_OWNED_ELSEWHERE each have a naming rule of their own, and role="presentation"/"none" removes a control unless it is still tabbable.
expectation: Each applicable control carries a programmatic label by one of the mechanisms helpers.getLabelMethod resolves, in its priority order: an associated <label>, aria-labelledby, aria-label, title, then placeholder. Any of the five satisfies this rule. Whether the weaker two are an appropriate primary label is a separate question, asked by form-control-programmatic-label-quality.

examples.explanation: The `<label for>` association gives the input a programmatic label.
No `<label>`, `aria-label`, or `aria-labelledby` — nothing programmatic names the field.

title: Form controls should have a label shown on screen
description: Flags form controls whose accessible name comes from placeholder, title, aria-label, or aria-labelledby pointing only at hidden text, none of which is a label shown on screen. Prefer a visible <label>, or aria-labelledby pointing at visible text.
applicability:
Applies to labelable native form controls exposed to assistive technologies:

- input (excluding type=hidden|submit|reset|button|image)
- select
- textarea

role="presentation"/"none" are excluded only when not focusable. A control not drawn on screen is excluded: transparent (opacity 0, its own or an ancestor's) or clipped away (as visually hidden text is), as a checkbox hidden behind a styled toggle is. It has no visible label to judge; its visible stand-in does. Only controls that have a programmatic name count: a control with none is form-control-programmatic-label-present's finding, not a question about how good its name is.
expectation:
If a control has a programmatic name, it should not come ONLY from:

- placeholder (non-empty)
- title (non-empty)
- aria-label
- aria-labelledby whose every referenced element is unrendered (hidden, display:none, visibility:hidden)

Prefer an associated <label> or aria-labelledby pointing at visible text.
reports:
- `labelMethod`: where the control's label comes from: `placeholder`, `title`, `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.
- `reasonCode`: `label_from_placeholder_primary`, `label_from_title_primary`, `label_from_aria_label_only` or `label_from_hidden_labelledby`.
- `sourceText`: the label text, up to 120 characters.
- `labelledbyTargets` (`label_from_hidden_labelledby`): the elements aria-labelledby points at (`#id`), with `hiddenBy` and, when an ancestor carries it, `hiddenByElement`, for a single target.

examples.explanation: A persistent `<label>` provides the name; `placeholder` is just a format hint here.
The control's only name comes from `placeholder`, which disappears once the user starts typing.
The control's only name comes from `title`, which is shown only on hover. Both give the control a name, so WCAG 4.1.2 is met; what is missing is a label shown to everyone, which is SC 3.3.2.

The control's only name comes from `aria-label`, which is never shown on screen. Visible text next to the field, such as a search button, may still tell sighted users what it is for, so this needs a look rather than a fail.

title: Form controls should not have multiple labels
description: Checks that a form control is associated with at most one <label> (by wrapping or by label[for]).
applicability: Applies to labelable form controls (input, excluding hidden/submit/reset/button/image; select; textarea).
expectation:
At most one <label> that can contribute to the control's accessible name is associated with it, as HTML's labeled control defines: a <label for="..."> whose value is the id of the first element with that id in the label's own tree, or a wrapping <label> without `for` whose first labelable descendant is the control (a label that both wraps and self-references via for counts once). Graded by whether the surplus labels actually compete for the name:

- PASS when an override (aria-labelledby / aria-label) supersedes every native <label>: the labels then contribute nothing to the name, so they cannot be ambiguous. A visible-label-vs-name mismatch is SC 2.5.3 Label in Name's concern, not this rule's.
- CANTTELL when two or more non-empty labels compete and there is no override: browsers join their text, in DOM order, into one name, and only a person can tell whether that joined name still makes sense ("Address Mailing address") or reads as noise.
- CANTTELL when one non-empty label is joined by empty label association(s) and there is no override: the name usually resolves to the real label, but handling of the empty association is not guaranteed across user agents.

All-empty associations with no override are a missing-name case (the sibling rule form-control-programmatic-label-present), not an ambiguity, so this rule stays silent.
reports:
- `labelCount`: how many labels are associated with the control. On the competing-labels case, only the non-empty ones are counted; on the empty-label case, the empty ones are counted too.
- `contributingLabelCount` (the empty-label case): how many of those labels have text, and so give the control its name.

examples.explanation: A single wrapping label; only one labelling mechanism applies.
Two separate `label[for]` elements both target the same control. Browsers join them into one name, "Address Mailing address", and only a person can tell whether it still reads well.

title: Heading levels must not skip a level
description: Checks that heading levels increase by at most one at a time in document order.
applicability: Applies whenever the page contains two or more heading elements (native <h1>-<h6>, or explicit role="heading" with aria-level; default level 2 per the ARIA spec when aria-level is absent/invalid). A native <hx> with a valid aria-level (a positive integer) takes that level, as browsers expose it; otherwise it takes its tag level. A native <hx> marked role="none" or "presentation" is still a heading when it can take focus or carries a global ARIA attribute, as WAI-ARIA's presentational roles conflict resolution has browsers ignore that role then. A custom element whose ElementInternals give it the heading role (this.attachInternals().role) counts as role="heading" does, at the level its aria-level attribute or its internals' ariaLevel give.
expectation: In the order assistive technology reads the page, each heading's level is no more than one greater than the level of the previous heading exposed to assistive technology. Jumping deeper by more than one level (e.g. an <h1> followed directly by an <h3>, skipping <h2>) breaks the document outline assistive technology users rely on when navigating by heading. Going back to a shallower level at any point is always fine.
reports:
- `fromLevel`: the level of the previous exposed heading (3 for an <h3>).
- `toLevel`: this heading's level, more than one deeper than `fromLevel`.
- `previousText`, `previousSelector`: the previous exposed heading, its text (shortened) and a selector for it.

examples.explanation: Each heading level increases by at most one at a time.
The heading level jumps from 1 to 3, skipping level 2.

title: Heading text should be descriptive, not a placeholder
description: Flags headings whose accessible name is a placeholder rather than a description of the content that follows: a generic word ("Heading", "Untitled"), a numbered template slot ("Section 2"), a filename, or a URL. A custom element whose ElementInternals give it the heading role (this.attachInternals().role), with no role attribute naming another, counts as a native element with that role does.

title: Text should be real text, not an image of text

description: Checks that an alt text is not identical to other visible text already present in its immediate parent element.

description: Flags , and

title: must have an alt attribute
description: Checks that elements provide an alt attribute to support a text alternative mechanism.
applicability: Applies to elements included in the accessibility tree. Images with role="presentation" or role="none" are excluded only when they are not focusable and have no global ARIA attribute, since presentational roles conflict resolution gives either one back its img role. Hidden images are excluded whether or not they are focusable.

title: alt text must be appropriate (manual review)
description: Flags elements with non-empty alt text for human review of appropriateness, and says when the alt looks like a file name, a web address, a placeholder, an "image of" opening or is very long.
applicability: Applies to elements whose alt attribute is present and non-empty. The element must be included in the accessibility tree, and a role attribute resolving to presentation/none (its first token naming a known role, matched case-insensitively) takes it out of scope unless it is focusable, which restores its role. An with no alt at all is img-alt-present's failure, and one with alt="" is img-alt-decorative's review.
expectation: Human review is required to confirm that the provided text alternative is accurate and appropriate. title: <input type="image"> must have an alt attribute

title: <input type="image"> text alternative must be appropriate (manual review)
description: Flags <input type="image"> elements with a non-empty text alternative (alt, aria-label, aria-labelledby or title) for human review of appropriateness. Says when the name looks like a file name, a web address, a placeholder, an "image of" opening or is very long.

An element whose alt is present but empty is left to input-image-alt-decorative, which asks about that case. The element must be included in the accessibility tree, and role="presentation"/"none" takes it out of scope unless it is focusable, which restores its role.
expectation: Human review is required to confirm that the provided text alternative is accurate and appropriate. Each occurrence lists every source present (data.details.sources), so the reviewer checks each one. The name is also checked for what the img-alt-quality rule checks in an alt (helpers.getTextAlternativeSignal): a file name, a web address, only symbols, a placeholder or generic word, an opening that says it is an image, or more than 150 characters. Such a name gets its own summary and hint; the finding stays `cantTell`.

- `reasonCode`: `TEXT_ALTERNATIVE_REVIEW`, whatever the signal.
- `name`: the control's text alternative as announced, from the first source that gives one.
- `sources`: every source that gives a non-empty text alternative, in the order they are used for the name. One item is `aria-labelledby`, `aria-label`, `alt` or `title`.

title: Fields marked invalid should have a shown error message
description: Checks that an element with aria-invalid has an error message in text: its aria-errormessage should name a shown element with text, and a field with no linked message is asked about.
applicability: Elements the page shows, in the accessibility tree and not disabled, whose `aria-invalid` says they are invalid: `true`, or a value ARIA reads as `true` (anything but `false`, `grammar`, `spelling` or empty). `grammar` and `spelling` mark text, not a value a user entered.
expectation:
The error is identified and described to the user in text (WCAG 3.3.1).

- `aria-errormessage` names an element that is shown and has text: pass.
- `aria-errormessage` names only elements that are hidden (`ERROR_MESSAGE_HIDDEN`): cantTell, leaning fail. ARIA requires the message to be shown while the field is invalid, and the page states it isn't; but, as for an empty message, the error may still be told in the label or next to the field, which meets 3.3.1.
- `aria-errormessage` names only shown elements with no text (`ERROR_MESSAGE_EMPTY`): cantTell. ARIA sets no MUST on the message's text, and the error may be told in the label or next to the field, which meets 3.3.1. When the field's `aria-describedby` gives a description, the error may be there: cantTell (`ERROR_MESSAGE_NOT_SHOWN_DESCRIBED`).
- `aria-errormessage` names no element of the page: cantTell (`ERROR_MESSAGE_TARGET_MISSING`); a script may add it.
- No `aria-errormessage`, and `aria-describedby` gives a description: pass.
- Neither: cantTell (`NO_ERROR_MESSAGE`). The error may be in the label or in text next to the field, which the markup doesn't tie to it; check that the user is told, in text, which field is in error and what is wrong.
- `aria-errormessage` names a message that is `aria-hidden` itself or inside an `aria-hidden` element: cantTell, leaning fail (`ERROR_MESSAGE_HIDDEN`, with `hiddenBy: 'aria-hidden'`). ARIA counts such an element as hidden, and requires a pertinent error message not to be.
- `aria-errormessage` names a shown message all of whose text is inside `aria-hidden` elements, while the message itself is not: cantTell (`ERROR_MESSAGE_ARIA_HIDDEN`). People who see it are told; screen reader users may not be.

An element counts as hidden when nobody sees it: `display: none`, `visibility: hidden`, `hidden`, a closed `<details>` or `content-visibility: hidden` on it or an ancestor; a message hidden with `visibility: hidden` whose text is brought back with `visibility: visible` is shown. Text is what the accessible name computation reads: an image's alt counts, and text hidden inside the message doesn't. The message may be named by id or set from script as an element (`ariaErrorMessageElements`).
reports:
- `ariaInvalid`: the attribute's value.
- `hiddenBy` (`ERROR_MESSAGE_HIDDEN`): `aria-hidden` when only aria-hidden hides the message; absent when nobody sees it.
- `errorMessageIds`: the ids `aria-errormessage` names, or [] for none.

- `for` names an element that can't be labelled: cantTell (`LABEL_FOR_NOT_LABELABLE`).

Either way the label labels nothing. Check which control it was meant for: that control may be named another way, which the name rules judge, or be left without the visible label meant for it.

title: Label in Name: accessible name contains visible text
description: Checks that when a control has a visible text label, the accessible name contains that visible label text.
applicability: Applies to controls named by aria-label or aria-labelledby, are visually rendered, and have visible label text this engine can extract deterministically, from an associated
expectation: The accessible name contains the visible label's words, adjacent and in order. In a browser, the label is also read as it shows: two boxes drawn side by side on one line with no space between them join their words (flex items "sure" and "a11y" read "surea11y"), and a name that holds either reading contains the label. The comparison is over words rather than characters: parenthesised text is dropped, case is folded, text is NFKC-normalised, and every character that is not a letter, digit or combining mark becomes a separator, so punctuation and spacing differences never decide the outcome. Invisible formatting characters (a soft hyphen, a zero-width space) and an apostrophe inside a word are removed instead, so "Down­load" is "Download" and "Don’t" is "Dont". Accents are not folded: "Déposer" stays one word, and a name that drops an accent ("Deposer") does not contain it. Four shapes markup cannot settle are reported as cantTell instead of fail: a word hyphenated differently in the two places; a visible word the author may have abbreviated, marked by its trailing period; visible text rendered through a known icon font (the DOM text is real words, but nothing readable actually renders); and a whole visible label of exactly one character that doesn't even appear inside the accessible name, which per ACT 2ee8b8 may be "non-text content" (e.g. "X" meaning "close") rather than literal text.
reports:
- `visibleLabel`, `accessibleName`: the visible label text and the accessible name, as found.
- `normalized.visibleLabel`, `normalized.accessibleName`: the same two texts as compared: parenthesised text dropped, case folded, Unicode normalised.
- `tokenized.visibleLabel`, `tokenized.accessibleName`: the words each text was split into, one word per item. The name must hold the label's words next to each other and in order.
- Each text is cut at 2,000 characters, with "…" after it, as an occurrence's `html` is, and each word list at its first 200 words.
- `labelSource`: where the visible label came from: `label` (an associated `<label>`), `self` (the control's own text), `value` (a button-type `<input>`'s value) or `aria-labelledby` (the elements it points at).
- `nameMechanism`: what gives the accessible name: `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.

description: Checks that the banner landmark (role="banner" or a non-nested <header>) is not nested inside another landmark region.

title: Page should have a main landmark
description: Checks that the page has at least one main landmark (role="main" or <main>).

title: Region and form roles must have an accessible name
description: Checks that an element given role="region" or role="form" has an accessible name, without which it is not exposed as a landmark.
applicability: Applies to elements whose role attribute resolves to region or form (its first known, non-abstract token, in any case: role="foo region" counts, role="search region" is a search landmark), and that are included in the accessibility tree. A custom element whose ElementInternals give it one of those roles (this.attachInternals().role), with no role attribute naming another, is in scope too: that is its default role, and no other rule checks it.

WAI-ARIA requires one ("Authors MUST give each element with role region a brief label", and the same for form), and without one the element is not exposed as a landmark at all, so the role the author asked for is lost. Reported at CANTTELL rather than FAIL: the requirement is WAI-ARIA's, not a WCAG Success Criterion's. Nothing false reaches assistive technology, which gets a plain container, so whether losing the landmark harms anyone depends on the page.

title: Landmarks with the same role must have unique names
description: Checks that when two or more landmarks share the same role, each has a distinct accessible name.
applicability: Applies whenever two or more landmark regions on the page share the same landmark role (banner, contentinfo, main, navigation, complementary, region, form, or search). A custom element whose ElementInternals give it a landmark role (this.attachInternals().role), with no role attribute naming another, is a landmark as a native element with that role is.
expectation: Among landmarks sharing a role, each has a distinct accessible name (via aria-label/aria-labelledby; landmarks are not named from content). Two same-role landmarks with the same name (including two both left unnamed) are indistinguishable to assistive technology users navigating by landmark. A shared name is reported as CANTTELL, never as a failure: the ARIA Authoring Practices allow one when the landmarks have the same content and purpose, such as pagination repeated above and below a table, which only a person can confirm. Two unnamed landmarks need names either way, and the same allowance then applies to those names.
reports:
- `role`: the landmark role the colliding landmarks share, such as `navigation`.
- `name`: the name they share, in lowercase with spacing collapsed. Empty when they are all unnamed.
- `groupSize`: how many landmarks of that role share that name.
- `others`: the other landmarks in the group, as the message names them (`<nav id="pages">`, with their text when they are unnamed).

title: Links in text blocks must be distinguishable from surrounding text without relying on color alone
description: Checks that a link inside a run of text is visually distinguishable from the surrounding text by a non-color cue (underline, font-weight or style, border, background, icon), and asks about links distinguished only by a >=3:1 color difference, which also need a hover and focus cue.
applicability:
Applies to links (`` and elements whose role attribute resolves to link: its first known role token, in any case, is `link`) that draw text (text other than white space in the link's flat tree and, where the page has a layout, a box with some area) and whose immediate parent element also has text with a letter or a digit beside it, on the link's own line (a `
`, or a child laid out as a block, starts another): a direct-child text node, or text in an inline element that is not a link, is not drawn invisibly, and is not an item of a flex or grid parent (i.e. the link sits inline within a run of plain text, not as a standalone item, e.g. not the sole content of a
  • nav item, nor one of a row of links separated by "|" or "·"). A custom element whose ElementInternals give it the link role (this.attachInternals().role), with no role attribute naming another, counts as a native element with that role does.
expectation:
A link inside a text block must be visually distinguishable from the surrounding text by at least one non-color means:

- text-decoration: underline, OR
- a different font-weight or font-style than the surrounding text, OR
- another visible mark on the link itself: a border, box-shadow or outline, a background color different from the surrounding one, a background image, an image or svg inside it, or a ::before/::after that draws something (content of its own, or an empty box painting a background, border, outline or shadow, as an underline drawn that way does), OR
- a mark on all of its content: bold, italic, underlined, bordered, a background unlike the surrounding text's (a code chip, <mark>), or raised or lowered (a footnote's <sup>).

A link with none of these is distinguished by color alone. When its color contrasts with the surrounding text by at least 3:1, technique G183 is met only if hover and focus also bring a non-color cue, which a static scan cannot see, so the link is reported as cantTell. Below 3:1, with contrast confidently computable, color is demonstrably the only cue and the link fails. The ratio between the link's color and the text's needs no background, so where only the background, or an effect applied alike to both, keeps it from being measured, two opaque text colors still decide it. Margin (`contrast-ratio`): of the links told apart by color alone that reach 3:1, the one closest to it, with its ratio unrounded. Those links are also asked about (the hover and focus cue), so the margin appears on a cantTell or fail result. Only a link within 10% of 3:1 (up to 3.3:1) counts as close. `measuredCount` counts the links whose only cue is color.
reports:
- `metrics.ratio` (a link set apart by color only): the contrast between the link's text color and the surrounding text's, as a ratio (3 for 3:1), against `metrics.threshold` (3).
- `metrics.ratioBeforeOpacity` (a link set apart by color only, under `ANCESTOR_OPACITY`): that ratio before an ancestor's opacity fades the link and the text alike, in place of `metrics.ratio`. The fading brings the two colors closer, so the ratio drawn may be lower: below 3:1 the link fails all the same, at 3:1 or more it is asked about with no lean toward pass, and it gives no margin.
- `colors.linkForegroundHex`, `colors.surroundingTextForegroundHex` (a link set apart by color only): the link's text color and the surrounding text's, as hex.
- `colorScheme` (a link with a background color of its own, on the canvas of a page that supports light and dark): `'light'` or `'dark'`, the scheme in which that background doesn't set it apart from the canvas around it, where it does in the other; the ratio and colors are that scheme's. Absent where it falls short in every scheme measured.
- `colorSchemesChecked` (the same link): the schemes it was compared in, where the page supports both and one could not be measured (its colors or the backgrounds around it may change with the scheme). A binding can scan again with the browser in the other scheme.

An <a> without an href is not a link and is not matched. An <a href>/<area href> whose explicit role is a known role other than link, a DPUB role inheriting from link, none or presentation is not a link and is not matched (ACT c487ae, Inapplicable Example 1). It is a generic phrase (`GENERIC_LINK_TEXT`) or a bare format name (`AMBIGUOUS_FORMAT_NAME`). - `linkKind`: what the link is made of (`helpers.getLinkKind`): `svg` for an `` in SVG; `image` for an ``, or a link whose content is only images (``, `

title: Lists must only directly contain list items
description: Checks that <ul>/<ol> elements only have <li>, <script>, or <template> as direct children.
applicability: Applies to <ul>/<ol> elements that have at least one direct element child or non-whitespace text directly inside them, and whose role is list: no role attribute, a role attribute resolving to list (its first token naming a known role, in any case), or one naming no known ARIA role. A <ul>/<ol> given another role (listbox, menubar, tablist, none, ...) is not a list, so its children follow that role's rules instead.
expectation: Every direct element child is <li>, <script>, or <template>. UNLESS it has an explicit role (its role attribute's first token naming a known role, matched in any case), in which case the explicit role wins over the tag entirely: a child is valid iff that role is "listitem" (so `<li role="presentation">`/`<li role="menuitem">` are invalid despite the <li> tag, and conversely a non-<li> element explicitly given `role="listitem"` or `role="foo LISTITEM"` is valid). A role attribute naming no known role leaves the tag to decide. A wrapper <div> used for styling (no role at all) still breaks list semantics the same as before. Non-whitespace text directly inside the list is an invalid child too: HTML allows only <li> and script-supporting elements there, and the text belongs to no list item. A child that does not belong FAILS only where the page shows an item the markup loses: the child is drawn as a list item (display list-item with a marker), or it wraps <li> elements that are, which HTML-AAM then maps to no list item. That is a relationship shown and not programmatically determinable (SC 1.3.1). Anything else (a heading or a separator between the items, loose text, an <li> whose role replaces listitem with no marker drawn) breaks HTML's content model, and H48 is only a sufficient technique: it is reported at CANTTELL, for a person to say whether the page shows it as one of the items. The marker is read from the computed style; jsdom does not resolve the list-style shorthand, so there `list-style: none` set that way still reads as a marker, and the finding fails as it would have before.
reports:
- `reasonCode`: `LIST_ITEM_ROLE_OVERRIDDEN` when every child that does not belong is an <li> whose explicit role replaces listitem (`<li role="presentation">`, `role="none"`, `role="group"`...), and `LIST_INVALID_CHILD` for any other child: an element that is not an <li>, or text. A list with both is `LIST_INVALID_CHILD`.
- `element`: the list's tag name, `ul` or `ol`.
- `invalidChildren`: the children that do not belong in the list, one tag name per child (`#text` for text placed directly inside).
- `overriddenRoles`: with `LIST_ITEM_ROLE_OVERRIDDEN`, the role of each such <li>, in order.
- `element` is a stable contract, unlike the rest of `data.details`.

A `<div>` between the `<ul>` and its `<li>` leaves the bulleted item in no list.
A `<div>` is a direct child of `<ul>` alongside the `<li>`, but it is not drawn as a list item: whether a WCAG criterion fails depends on whether the page shows it as one.

title: Listboxes have an accessible name
description: Checks that elements with role="listbox" expose a non-empty accessible name.
applicability: Applies to elements whose role attribute resolves to listbox: its first token naming a known role, matched in any case, is listbox, so role="foo listbox" and role="LISTBOX" count while role="link listbox" (a link) does not. The element must be included in the accessibility tree. An element with the matching implicit role but no role attribute is out of scope. A custom element whose ElementInternals give it the role (this.attachInternals().role), with no role attribute naming another, is in scope too: that is its default role, and no other rule checks it.
expectation: The element has a non-empty accessible name from aria-label, from an aria-labelledby that resolves to non-empty text, or from title. role="listbox" is name-from-author-only, so subtree text is never accepted: text sitting inside a custom listbox widget is not reliably exposed as its name. On a labelable element (<select multiple role="listbox">) an associated <label> counts as well.

examples.explanation: `aria-label` names the listbox.
No accessible name from any supported mechanism.

title: List items must be inside a list container
description: Checks that <li> elements are contained by <ul>, <ol>, <menu>, or an element with role="list".
applicability: Applies to <li> elements that have a parent element.
expectation: The parent is <ul>/<ol>/<menu> with no role override (all three have the implicit role list), or an element with an explicit role of "list", "directory" (deprecated, but a required parent of listitem in WAI-ARIA 1.2), "presentation", or "none". An <li> used outside a real list container (e.g. as a generic flex/grid item under a <div>) is not exposed as a list item to assistive technologies. It FAILS where the page still draws the <li> as a list item (display list-item with a marker): an item a reader sees that the markup puts in no list, a relationship not programmatically determinable (SC 1.3.1). An <li> drawn with no marker, as a plain layout box, shows no list, so the broken content model is reported at CANTTELL (H48 is only a sufficient technique) for a person to say whether it reads as a list. jsdom does not resolve the list-style shorthand, so there `list-style: none` set that way still reads as a marker.
reports:
- `reasonCode`: `LIST_ROLE_OVERRIDDEN` when the parent is a <ul>, <ol> or <menu> whose explicit role replaces list (`<ul role="tablist">`), `LISTITEM_INVALID_PARENT` otherwise. Both fail where the <li> is drawn as a list item, and are asked about where it is not.
- `parentElement`: the tag name of the `<li>`'s parent, the container it is in instead of a list.
- `parentRole`: with `LIST_ROLE_OVERRIDDEN`, the parent's role.
- `parentElement` is a stable contract, unlike the rest of `data.details`.

`<li>` has no `<ul>`/`<ol>`/`role="list"` ancestor, yet the browser draws it with a bullet: the page shows a list item the markup leaves in no list.

title: Live regions should be able to announce status messages
description: Flags a live region hidden from assistive technology or left busy, and, with the live-region hook, one added with its text or shown and filled at once, for manual review.
applicability: Live regions the page draws: elements whose aria-live is polite or assertive, or, without an aria-live, whose role is status, log or alert, and <output> elements. aria-live="off" turns any of them off. A live region hidden with display: none, visibility: hidden or [hidden] is left out: a region waiting to be shown is the page at rest. A live region behind an open modal <dialog>, which the browser makes inert, is included, though other rules leave that content out. With the live-region hook (liveRegionHookScript), also the live regions it saw given their text in a way that is commonly not announced, whether or not they are still on the page.
expectation:
WCAG 4.1.3: a status message can be presented to the user by assistive technology without receiving focus, which a live region does when its content changes while assistive technology can reach it.

- A drawn live region inside, or on, aria-hidden="true" or inert, or behind an open modal <dialog>: cantTell (`LIVE_REGION_HIDDEN`). It is out of the accessibility tree, so nothing it is given can be announced (behind the dialog, while the dialog is open).
- A live region with aria-busy="true" when the page was scanned: cantTell (`LIVE_REGION_BUSY`). Assistive technology may hold back its changes until aria-busy is cleared.
- Recorded by the hook, a live region added to the page with its text already in it, other than role="alert": cantTell (`LIVE_REGION_INSERTED_WITH_CONTENT`). Screen readers commonly announce changes to a region they already know, not a new region's content.
- Recorded by the hook, a live region that was hidden and was shown and given its text in the same task: cantTell (`LIVE_REGION_SHOWN_AND_FILLED`). It was not in the accessibility tree when the text arrived.
- Otherwise: pass.

Check whether the page uses the region for status messages, and that it is in the page, shown and reachable, before its text changes.
reports:
- `politeness`: the region's, `polite` or `assertive`.
- `messageKind`: the kind of message the region declares it carries, from its role and live-region attributes, never from its text: `status` (role status, an <output>, or aria-live="polite" with aria-atomic="true"), `alert` (role alert, or aria-live="assertive"), `log` (role log), `progress` (role progressbar, or a <progress>), or `unknown` (any other live region, such as a plain aria-live="polite"). A role, given or the element's own, wins over aria-live.
- `hiddenBy`: for `LIVE_REGION_HIDDEN`, `aria-hidden`, `inert`, or `modal` for a region behind an open modal <dialog>. A region behind the dialog is `modal` whatever else hides it (inert or aria-hidden on it or above it, with or without includeHiddenElements): while the dialog is open, it is the cause in effect.
- `hiddenByElement`: for `aria-hidden` or `inert` on an ancestor, that ancestor (`<div id="app">`).
- `text`: for the hook's two findings, the text the region was given (up to 300 characters).
- `removed`: for the hook's two findings, true when the region was no longer on the page when it was scanned; the occurrence is then on the document element, and `region` describes it (`tag`, `role`, `id`).
